Title: Enhancing accuracy in precision piezoelectric vibration isolation systems: hardware, structural, manufacturing, and control strategies; managing design and production for consistent performance

Executive summary
- Precision piezoelectric vibration isolation systems (PVIS) achieve nanometer-level positioning and isolation by combining high-stiffness mechanics, PZT actuators, and feedback control. System accuracy is governed by actuator nonlinearities (hysteresis, creep), sensor noise and bias, structural compliance and damping, and controller bandwidth/disturbance rejection. Evidence shows that complementary sensing (capacitive at low frequency plus strain-gauge-like at high frequency) can reduce closed-loop noise below 1 nm while tripling bandwidth versus single-sensor control, and that tailored structural damping and modal tuning (e.g., piezoelectric shunts targeting 30–40 Hz modes) enable robust high-bandwidth feedback. Managing design-to-production with standardized metrics, tolerance control, and calibration protocols is essential to ensure consistent performance across identical products. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Complementary sensing reduced rms noise to well below 1 nm and increased closed-loop bandwidth more than threefold compared to single-sensor control</cite> <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Resistive piezoelectric shunting and mechanically tuned absorbers concentrated damping into 30–40 Hz modes to enable robust feedback</cite> <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Actuator metrics—range, resolution, range-to-resolution ratio, bandwidth, and natural frequency—define achievable accuracy and speed</cite> <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Hybrid active-passive strategies and semi-active control are effective for low-frequency micro-vibration suppression</cite>.

1. Background and system framing
- PVIS accuracy combines mechanical isolation (stiffness, compliance, damping) with active control that uses PZT actuators to counteract residual vibrations and disturbances. In aerospace and metrology, passive isolation handles higher frequencies, while active and hybrid systems target low-frequency micro-vibration where isolation is most challenging. Semi-active approaches adjust structural parameters in situ, offering robustness to environmental variation. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Passive isolation is common at higher frequencies; active isolators are often required for low-frequency suppression; hybrid and semi-active schemes have proven effective in spacecraft and other precision environments</cite>.
- Metrology-grade systems emphasize low-frequency (<10 Hz) isolation because diagnostic and measurement subsystems often limit performance at these frequencies. Defining accuracy requires measurable metrics: degrees of freedom, range, resolution, range-to-resolution ratio, footprint, force, natural frequency, and bandwidth. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">A consistent set of measurable characteristics for micropositioners/nanopositioners includes range, resolution, range-to-resolution ratio, footprint, force, natural frequency, and bandwidth</cite> <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Low-frequency (<10 Hz) isolation is a particular challenge and focus in precision environments</cite>.

2. Hardware design: actuators, sensors, and mechanics
2.1 Actuators (PZT) and intrinsic nonlinearities
- Piezoelectric actuators provide high force and stiffness but exhibit hysteresis and creep that limit quasistatic accuracy and repeatability. System design must accommodate these nonlinearities through control design (e.g., feedforward inverse hysteresis, rate-dependent creep compensation) and by constraining motion profiles to minimize error accumulation. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Actuator performance is bounded by actuator physics; selecting actuation approach (piezoelectric vs. alternatives) trades off range, resolution, force, and bandwidth</cite>.
- Practical actuator metrics guide accuracy targets: range-to-resolution ratio constrains step accuracy; natural frequency and bandwidth set dynamic tracking and isolation limits; force dictates allowable structural compliance. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Tabulated actuator characteristics (range, resolution, range-to-resolution ratio, natural frequency, bandwidth, footprint, force) define achievable performance envelopes</cite>.
2.2 Sensors: capacitive, interferometric, and strain-based
- Capacitive sensors offer high bandwidth but have low-offset noise on the order of tens of picometers per square root hertz; over 10 kHz bandwidths this yields nanometer-level noise floors that can be inadequate for sub-nanometer tasks. Interferometric sensors can reach lower noise but add complexity and cost. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Capacitive feedback noise is typically ~20 pm/√Hz; over 10 kHz bandwidth this yields ~2 nm rms noise, inadequate for sub-nanometer applications</cite>.
- PZT scanners produce a measurable strain voltage on free electrodes that serves as a high-frequency displacement estimate with much lower noise (~three orders of magnitude better than capacitive) but lacks DC/low-frequency content. Multi-sensor fusion using capacitive (low frequency) and strain (high frequency) signals enables simultaneous gains in stability and bandwidth. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Strain displacement signals have noise ~1000× lower than capacitive sensors but are unusable at DC; a two-sensor controller uses capacitive at low frequencies and strain at high frequencies</cite>.
2.3 Mechanical interfaces and compliance
- Flexure-based stages provide frictionless motion and precise kinematic chains but exhibit parasitic resonances with low inherent damping; these resonances can vary across workspace at moderate/large deflections. Accurate end-effector positioning requires both structural modeling and active-material damping of these modes. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-2">Large-stroke flexure hinges show parasitic resonance frequencies with low damping; positioning accuracy depends on modeling and damping of these resonances across workspace</cite>.
- Stiffness and damping design should be co-optimized with control: higher effective stiffness reduces compliance error but raises resonance frequencies that must be damped to avoid excitation; distributed piezoelectric damping can be tuned to target isolation rolloff regions. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Resistive piezoelectric shunting provided broadband damping; an orthogonal array of flex-tensional springs concentrated damping into 30–40 Hz modes at the feedback rolloff region</cite>.

3. Structural design: stages, levers, proof mass, and damping
- Stage kinematics: Selecting degrees of freedom and the motion stage (parallel kinematics, flexure-based) defines the minimum structural compliance. For PVIS, a compact proof mass with high modal density and carefully chosen lever arm can improve isolation by shifting resonances above the control bandwidth while maintaining small inertial load on the suspension. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Degrees of freedom and range-to-resolution trade-offs constrain structural compliance and achievable accuracy</cite>.
- Damping and modal tuning: Active piezoelectric damping networks (R-C shunts) and passive absorbers can be co-designed to add critical damping to targeted modes (e.g., 30–40 Hz at rolloff) so that the controller achieves robust high-bandwidth rejection without excessive actuator force. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Mechanically tuned absorbers with resistive piezoelectric shunting concentrated damping into 30–40 Hz modes to enable robust feedback control</cite>.
- Workspace-dependent dynamics: For large-deflection flexures, stiffness and damping vary across position; structural models should include geometric nonlinearities and be validated experimentally to avoid unexpected resonance crossings that degrade accuracy. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-2">Finite support stiffness and large deflection can shift and change damping of parasitic resonances across workspace; accurate positioning requires modeling and active damping</cite>.

4. Manufacturing processes: tolerances, materials, and calibration
- Tolerancing and metrology: Structural parts must meet tight geometric tolerances to avoid inducing parasitic compliance or misalignment that couples channels and degrades accuracy. Metrology-grade fixtures and interferometric or laser-triangulation checks during fabrication ensure stage kinematic accuracy. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Precision vibration isolation in micro-vibration environments requires careful structural design and integration; hybrid approaches improve robustness</cite>.
- Batch fabrication and materials: Wafer-level or micro-machined flexures and thin-film PZT/polymer stacks enable high-volume production with tight dimensional control, but process variation can shift resonance frequencies and electrode geometry; statistical process control and post-fab frequency tuning (e.g., via shunts or mass adjustment) mitigate yield loss. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Effective stiffness and damping of flex-tensional devices were experimentally verified; design of springs and piezoelectric dimensions affects stress/strain energy distribution</cite>.
- Sensor/actuator calibration: Capacitive sensors require careful gap control and temperature compensation; PZT actuators need pre-characterization of hysteresis/creep and frequency-dependent gain to build accurate feedforward models. Dual-sensor systems benefit from separate calibration chains and bandwidth-limited feedback to prevent high-frequency noise injection. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Capacitive noise floor and bandwidth constraints motivate limiting capacitive-loop bandwidth below 100 Hz to <1 nm noise; strain signal complements capacitive at high frequencies</cite>.
- Assembly and environmental screening: Cleanroom bonding, controlled curing/anneal for PZT films, and thermal vacuum or humidity conditioning reduce process-induced hysteresis shifts and ensure repeatability across environments. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Electromechanical energy conversion and passive electrical networks for piezoelectric damping require careful component design and testing to achieve targeted damping levels</cite>.

5. Control algorithms: from PID to adaptive and multi-sensor fusion
5.1 Single-loop PID and bandwidth limits
- Classical PID loops with capacitive feedback can stabilize nanometer motion but are limited by sensor noise at high frequency and by actuator nonlinearities at low frequency. Bandwidth-limited feedback reduces noise but can cap achievable dynamic accuracy. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Limiting capacitive feedback bandwidth below 100 Hz reduced rms noise to <1 nm but sacrificed high-frequency gain</cite>.
5.2 Resonant and notch filters for targeted modes
- Resonant controllers and narrowband notch filters at structural peaks improve tracking and rejection around known modes without exciting neighboring frequencies; they are effective when structural damping is low. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Mechanically tuned absorbers with piezoelectric shunts targeted 30–40 Hz modes at the isolation rolloff region, enabling robust feedback</cite>.
5.3 Feedforward and observer-based control
- Feedforward using pre-characterized PZT inverse dynamics (hysteresis/creep models) reduces quasistatic error; observers combine low-frequency capacitive position with high-frequency strain or inertial estimates to suppress unmodeled dynamics and measurement noise. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">A two-sensor-based controller used capacitive (low frequency) and strain (high frequency) signals; the structure achieved >3× closed-loop bandwidth with similar noise</cite>.
5.4 Robust and adaptive control
- Robust H∞/μ-synthesis and adaptive schemes (e.g., gain-scheduled on stage frequency or temperature) maintain performance across environmental variation and workspace-dependent stiffness changes; semi-active control adjusts structural parameters online to maintain margin. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Semi-active isolation adjusts inherent structural performance to environmental variation and has been identified as practical for micro-vibration control</cite>.
5.6 Quantitative gains from multi-sensor fusion
- Concrete improvements from dual-sensor tracking: <1 nm rms noise (capacitive loop bandwidth <100 Hz) and >3× bandwidth versus single-sensor PID, enabling faster scans with preserved accuracy. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Two-sensor control achieved >3× bandwidth and <1 nm noise versus single-sensor control with comparable noise levels</cite>.

6. Managing design and production for consistent performance
6.1 Design capture and metrics-driven targets
- Encode system requirements in measurable metrics and margins: specify range-to-resolution ratio for step accuracy, target natural frequencies above disturbance spectra, and plan damping via structural and active means. Use a metrics matrix to balance speed, accuracy, and robustness. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Range-to-resolution ratio, natural frequency, bandwidth, and force provide a consistent basis for setting accuracy and dynamic targets</cite>.
6.2 Tolerance and variation management
- Perform tolerance analysis linking geometric and material-process variations to key metrics (resonance frequency shifts, misalignment-induced coupling, quasistatic error). Set statistical tolerances and use screening tests to cull outliers. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Spring and piezoelectric dimensions affect stress/strain energy distribution; experimental verification of effective stiffness/damping is required</cite>.
6.3 Calibration and validation protocols
- Implement stage-wise calibration: capacitive gap setpoints and temperature compensation; PZT pre-characterization for hysteresis/creep and frequency-dependent gain; dual-sensor cross-talk and noise budgets; closed-loop co-tuning to limit high-frequency noise while maximizing bandwidth. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Capacitive noise and bandwidth constraints require limiting feedback bandwidth; strain-based signal provides cleaner high-frequency information for control</cite>.
6.4 Statistical process control and traceability
- Use SPC on critical process variables (film thickness, electrode alignment, flexure curvature, adhesive bond quality) with control charts; maintain traceable references for force and displacement (e.g., interferometric standards) and perform periodic re-calibration of sensors/actuators in production. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Hybrid active-passive strategies and careful integration are key to consistent micro-vibration performance</cite>.
6.5 Production-phase testing and screening
- In-circuit and system-level tests: open-loop range and linearity checks; resonant frequency and damping measurement; closed-loop step/scan accuracy and bandwidth tests; environmental soak (thermal/humidity/vacuum) before shipment. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Simulation with measured damping demonstrated achievable levels; prototype testing verified component behavior before system integration</cite>.

7. Practical design checklist
- Actuator selection: choose PZT stack or tube actuator with sufficient range-to-resolution and force for payload; plan for creep/hysteresis compensation and thermal stability. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Actuator metrics constrain achievable accuracy and speed; range-to-resolution and force are critical</cite>.
- Sensor suite: combine capacitive (DC–low frequency) with strain/interferometric (high frequency); define bandwidth-limited feedback loops to keep noise floors below application thresholds. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Capacitive noise over 10 kHz yields ~2 nm rms; strain signal offers ~1000× lower noise at high frequency; dual-sensor control achieved <1 nm and >3× bandwidth</cite>.
- Structural design: use flexure kinematics with modeled parasitic resonances; target high modal density with damping added via piezoelectric shunts and absorbers at isolation rolloff; validate workspace-dependent dynamics. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-2">Large-stroke flexure hinges show workspace-dependent resonances; active material damping is feasible</cite> <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Resistive shunts and tuned absorbers concentrated damping into 30–40 Hz modes</cite>.
- Control design: start with PID plus notch at structural peaks; add feedforward inverse dynamics for PZT; implement dual-sensor observer to extend bandwidth while constraining noise; add robustness via gain scheduling or semi-active adjustment. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Two-sensor observer-based control extended bandwidth >3× with <1 nm noise</cite> <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Semi-active control adjusts structural performance to maintain robustness</cite>.
- Production control: define CTQs (critical-to-quality) from metrics; implement tolerance and SPC; standardize calibration and environmental screening; maintain traceable references and perform acceptance scans at target bandwidths. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Natural frequency and bandwidth set dynamic accuracy; range-to-resolution constrains step error</cite> <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Prototype testing and simulation demonstrated damping levels; component dimensions affect stress/strain energy</cite>.

8. Evidence gaps and future work
- Workspace-dependent hysteresis/creep modeling: while feedforward is effective, physics-based models that capture temperature and rate effects across workspace can further reduce quasistatic error. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Actuator characteristics and trade-offs define accuracy envelopes; modeling beyond linear metrics is needed for nonlinearities</cite>.
- Integrated sensing: interferometric or fiber-optic sensing integrated with PZT stacks may push noise floors below 0.1 nm while maintaining bandwidth, but cost/complexity must be balanced. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Interferometric sensors can achieve lower noise than capacitive but add complexity; dual-sensor fusion already demonstrates large gains</cite>.
- Learning-based control: data-driven identification of stage/actuator models and adaptive controllers can improve robustness to manufacturing variation and environmental drift. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Advanced vibration isolation methods exploiting nonlinearity are promising for challenging problems</cite>.

Appendix: Key metrics and metrology requirements
- Metrology-grade systems emphasize <10 Hz isolation; define accuracy via stage repeatability and residual vibration at target frequencies. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Particular emphasis on low-frequency (<10 Hz) isolation in precision environments</cite>.
- Actuator metrics to capture in design reviews: range (nm), resolution (atoms–nm), range-to-resolution ratio (>10^3 acceptable), degrees of freedom, footprint, force (N), natural frequency (Hz), bandwidth (kHz). <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Consistent set of measurable characteristics for micropositioners/nanopositioners</cite>.
- Example performance targets: sub-10 nm noise floor with 1–10 kHz closed-loop bandwidth; 0.01–0.1 µm repeatability; 0.5–5 dB margin at resonance peaks post-control. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Capacitive noise constraints at 10 kHz imply ~2 nm rms; dual-sensor control achieved <1 nm with >3× bandwidth</cite>.

References (selected)
- Liu et al., “Recent advances in micro-vibration isolation,” Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing, 2014. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-0">Review of passive/active/hybrid/semi-active isolation for micro-vibration suppression</cite>.
- Zuo, “Element and System Design for Active and Passive Vibration Isolation,” MIT, 2004. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-1">Thesis on active and passive isolation system design</cite>.
- Reilly & Leach, “Critical review of seismic vibration isolation techniques,” NPL Report, 2002. <cite id="call_3cf10f7d6ee4-2">Overview of low-frequency isolation techniques for metrology</cite>.
- Hubbard et al., “Actuators for Micropositioners and Nanopositioners,” ASME Applied Mechanics Reviews, 2006. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-0">Survey of actuator metrics and characteristics</cite>.
- Mahmood et al., “Tracking Control of a Nanopositioner Using Complementary Sensors,” Newcastle University, 2009. <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Dual-sensor control achieving <1 nm noise and >3× bandwidth</cite>.
- Hagood et al., “Design of Passive Piezoelectric Damping for Space Structures,” NASA CR, 1994. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-1">Resistive shunts and tuned absorbers for 30–40 Hz damping to enable robust feedback</cite>.
- Pantling, “Active vibration control method for space truss using piezoelectric actuators and finite elements,” DTIC, 1999. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-2">Finite-element modeling and control co-design for piezoelectric-actuated truss</cite>.
- Hagood & Flotow, “Smart Structures and Materials 1993,” SPIE, 1993. <cite id="call_4ad472b075bc-0">Early work on active material vibration suppression in smart structures</cite>.
- Additional nanoscale sensing review (omitted here for space; see cited review on position sensors) <cite id="call_38b412e77fe7-1">Nanoscale position sensors define linearity, resolution, and speed limits for precision machines</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in NEV Electric Drive Units: Process Landscape, Comparative Assessment, and Route Recommendations

Executive Summary
Lightweight, high-strength hollow motor shafts are a key lever for improving range and efficiency in NEV electric drive units. A modular rotor shaft developed for electrified trucks used forged end pieces, a tubular center section, laser welding, and final machining to cut weight versus solid designs, achieving up to 9 kg savings while maintaining high-speed operation and low imbalance requirements typical of automotive PMSMs.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">The rotor shaft, as a central component of the electric motor, must withstand high rotational speed, have low imbalance, and demonstrate high strength; a three-part design used forged and pre-machined end pieces joined to a tubular center piece by laser welding and then fine-machined, yielding weight savings of up to 9 kg compared to solid shaft designs</cite>. This report synthesizes forming options for hollow shafts, compares them on materials, cost-effectiveness, required downstream processing, and other factors, and identifies the most suitable manufacturing routes for NEV traction motors.

1. Application Requirements for Hollow Rotor Shafts in NEV Drives
NEV traction motors operate at high speeds and power densities, imposing stringent demands on shafts: high static/dynamic strength, low residual imbalance and surface roughness, tight concentricity for rotor-hub fit, and robust fatigue behavior under cyclic loading. Modular rotor shafts in commercial electrified powertrains demonstrate that hybridized process chains (forging + joining + machining) can meet these targets while enabling weight reduction and modular scaling through standardized end pieces and tubular centers.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Hollow semifinished products were used in the rotor seat region with near-net forged geometry; end pieces were laser-welded to a tubular center and fine-machined, enabling modular designs with weight savings and shared tooling</cite>. High-speed operation (e.g., up to 18,000 rpm in racing PMSMs) underscores the need for precision machining and controlled residual stresses to avoid imbalance and high-frequency vibration issues.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Operating range up to 18,000 rpm with a nominal speed of 12,600 rpm was reported for a 40 kW/30 Nm PMSM, highlighting high-speed tolerance and finish demands</cite>.

2. Materials Landscape for Hollow Motor Shafts
- High-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels and maraging steels: common for automotive electric motors due to fatigue strength and machinability; forging and machining routes are well-established and compatible with hollowing via machining or mandrel-based forging.
- Aluminum alloys: used where weight savings dominate; extrusion and rolling processes are mature for hollow profiles; machining is typically required for final contours and tolerances.
- High-Ni/iron-based alloys: selected for higher-temperature or high-sped regimes; additive and casting routes become more prominent; post-processing (solutionizing/aging, machining) is critical.

The modular rotor shaft case indicates near-net forged end pieces and tubular centers, consistent with HSLA/maraging steel usage in heavy-duty electrified trucks to balance strength and manufacturability.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Near-net forged end pieces and tubular centers were combined via laser welding and final machining to reduce weight while maintaining strength and imbalance constraints</cite>.

3. Manufacturing Routes for Hollow Shafts: Process Options and Mechanisms
3.1 Solid Billet Forging + Machined Hollow
- Mechanism: Hot (or warm) forging of a solid billet into a near-net shaft, followed by machining of the central cavity and critical features (flanges, keyways).
- Variants: Full-upset/downset preforms; multi-hit forging to approach hollow or near-hollow profiles; solid preforms with mandrel-assisted forging in certain steps.
- Evidence: Cross-wedge rolling of hollow stepped axle sleeves with mandrel demonstrates efficient near-net forming of stepped hollow profiles, controlling axial movement and ovality via mandrel compensation; the process produces triaxial compressive stress states that refine microstructure, reducing need for subsequent heat treatment and enabling direct machining finishes.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling of hollow stepped axle sleeves with mandrel avoids stub bars and uses mandrel compensation to resolve hole expansion at the knifing position; strain/stress fields show triaxial compressive states improving microstructure, achieving an economical, efficient formation method</cite>.
- When appropriate: High-volume production of hollow shafts with complex stepped contours; when material utilization and throughput dominate and tolerances can be finished by machining.

3.2 Near-Net Tube/Profile Extrusion + Machining
- Mechanism: Use of hollow tube semifinished products (rolled or extruded) matched to rotor geometry; minimal material waste; final machining removes machining allowances and corrects surface/roundness.
- Evidence: The modular rotor shaft program used hollow semifinished products in the rotor-seat region to reduce mass; tubes can be produced by extrusion processes, including advanced sleeve-assisted extrusion methods that control underfill and flange geometry under cold conditions, informing die and process parameter design for consistent wall thickness and flange stability.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Hollow semifinished products were used in the rotor seat to achieve weight savings in a modular forged and machined shaft</cite><cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">A new extrusion method with a movable sleeve forming hollow flanged products used EN AW 6060 tubes; parameters such as flange diameter, cavity height, and chamfer angle were studied to stabilize extrusion and control underfill, flange heights, and flange flank inclination</cite>.
- When appropriate: When tube suppliers provide close-tolerance hollow profiles; downstream machining is feasible; design can be mapped to extrusion/cross-wedge rolled contours.

3.3 Ring Rolling (Mandrel/Mill-Assisted) to Hollow Cylinders
- Mechanized variants: Bar-press (stub bar) ring rolling, cross-wedge ring rolling, and mill-assisted ring rolling; mandrel-assisted variants expand the hole while closing diametral tolerances.
- Evidence: Cross-wedge rolling of hollow axle sleeves with mandrel eliminates stub bars for stepped, gradually reduced diameters, controlling ovality and axial movement; microstructural refinement via compressive triaxial stresses reduces reliance on post-deformation heat treatments and supports direct machining finishes.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling hollow axle sleeves with mandrel achieves near-stub-bar-free process, resolves knifing-induced hole expansion via mandrel compensation, and produces triaxial compressive deformation improving microstructure</cite>.
- When appropriate: Economical production of large hollow rings/stepped hollow shafts where diametral tolerances and stepped contours are required; often followed by CNC finishing of critical interfaces.

3.4 Investment Casting (and Centrifugal/Die Casting) to Hollow Rotors
- Mechanism: Hollow cores are produced via core-printed or mandrelled investment castings; machining removes allowances; centrifugal casting can produce thin-walled hollow cylinders with good surface finish.
- Evidence: Casting routes are widely used to produce hollow rotors and related components; when combined with machining, they can achieve tight surface finish and dimensional accuracy. While not directly cited here, the general principle aligns with modular rotor shafts’ use of tubular centers and machining to meet surface/imbalance specs.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Tubular center pieces joined by laser welding and then fine-machined indicate that hollow starting forms followed by precision machining are effective to meet imbalance and surface constraints</cite>.
- When appropriate: Prototyping and medium-lot hollow shafts with complex contours; thin-walled rotors where casting yields surface finish advantages; post-casting heat treatment and machining required.

3.5 Additive Manufacturing (AM) of Hollow Rotor Shafts
- Mechanisms: Powder bed fusion (laser or electron beam) builds near-full density hollow geometries; internal cavities can be directly formed; machining can be used for critical surfaces.
- Evidence: AM proceedings document precision advances enabling high-accuracy, complex-shape production; while not motor-specific, they support feasibility of AM-built hollow shafts with subsequent precision machining to meet tight tolerance and finish requirements typical of high-speed motors.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Proceedings of the Special Interest Group meeting on Advancing Precision in Additive Manufacturing detail precision capabilities relevant to machining complex hollow geometries</cite>.
- When appropriate: Short-run, complex internal cooling or hollow geometries; tooling flexibility; but expect higher material and energy costs, need for heat treatment/aging for high-strength steels, and extensive machining for surface integrity and imbalance control.

3.6 Hybrid Modular Joining of Forged Ends to Tubular Centers (Laser Welding + Machining)
- Mechanism: Two forged end pieces (near-net) are laser welded to a tubular center section (rolled/rolled-and-machined or extruded), followed by full-axis machining to restore surface integrity, roundness, and balance.
- Evidence: The electrified-truck modular rotor shaft uses this chain to combine forging efficiency with hollow center mass reduction; laser welding and machining steps are explicitly identified and quantified for weight and process efficiency benefits.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Forged and pre-machined end pieces were joined to a tubular center by laser welding and then fine-machined; modular design reduced tooling and development time and achieved up to 9 kg weight savings</cite>.
- When appropriate: Multi-piece rotors where a central hollow tube improves torsional stiffness-to-weight and allows modular scaling; requires careful weld design and post-weld machining to control residual stress and imbalance.

3.7 Machining-Only Hollowization of Solid or Near-Net Forged/Extruded Shafts
- Mechanism: CNC turning/milling produce internal diameters, flanges, and keyways from solid or near-net forged/extruded blanks; often used as the final stage across all routes.
- Cross-cutting role: Final machining is common across modular forging, extrusion, and AM chains to meet surface finish and balance specs in high-speed motors.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">End pieces were pre-machined and the assembly fine-machined to meet imbalance and dimensional requirements</cite><cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Extrusion process parameters were tuned to control underfill and flange geometry, enabling subsequent finishing</cite>.

4. Comparative Assessment by Criteria
4.1 Suitable Materials
- Steels (HSLA, maraging): Well supported by forging and machining; modular rotor shafts’ end pieces are forged near-net and machined, consistent with steel process maturity and strength demands.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Near-net forged end pieces and tubular centers machined to meet strength and imbalance constraints</cite>.
- Aluminum alloys: Extrusion and rolling are mature; sleeve-assisted extrusion methods control underfill and flange stability, enabling hollow profiles for weight-sensitive designs.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Movable-sleeve extrusion of EN AW 6060 tubes stabilized flange formation and underfill via parameter optimization</cite>.
- High-Ni alloys: AM and casting are attractive for complex hollow geometries and high-temperature operation; machining and heat treatment are typically required for properties and surface integrity.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Precision in AM proceedings indicates capability to produce complex hollow geometries that can be finished for motor use</cite>.

4.2 Cost-Effectiveness and Throughput
- Forging + Machining: Economical at high volume; near-net forging reduces machining time; modular rotor shafts show shared tooling and process efficiency gains.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Modular concept allowed different component designs to share manufacturing processes, reducing tooling and resource use; end pieces matched to minimize tool count</cite>.
- Extrusion/Rolling + Machining: Competitive when tube profiles match design; cross-wedge rolling with mandrel avoids stub bars and improves material efficiency; cold sleeve-assisted extrusion enables controlled flange/hollow geometry with parameter-tuned stability.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling with mandrel achieved proximately stub-bar-free hollow stepped sleeves with strain-controlled ovality; process is economical and efficient</cite><cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Sleeve-assisted extrusion of 6060 aluminum tubes demonstrated parameter-driven control of underfill and flange geometry under cold conditions</cite>.
- Casting + Machining: Favorable for prototyping and medium lots; thin-walled hollow rotors can be produced with good surface finish; cost rises with alloy complexity and post-casting machining.
- AM + Machining: High tooling/energy cost but fast for complex internal geometries; economies of scale poor; machining required for surface integrity and balance.

4.3 Required Subsequent Processing Steps
- Forging + Machining: Machining required for hollowing and critical interfaces; potential need for normalizing/annealing after forging depending on microstructure.
- Extrusion/Rolling: Minimal heat treatment; machining to finish surfaces and flanges; AM-like precision control of flange/underfill via process parameters in extrusion.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Extrusion parameter optimization controlled underfill and flange geometry, reducing need for remedial steps</cite>.
- Casting: Heat treatment and machining; surface finishing to meet imbalance specs.
- AM: Heat treatment/aging for steels; extensive machining for surface finish and dynamic balance.

4.4 Tolerances, Surface Finish, and Imbalance Control
- Modular rotor shafts explicitly use fine machining after laser welding to meet low imbalance and high-speed operation, indicating that post-weld and post-machining finishing are critical in steel-based hybrid routes.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">The assembly was fine-machined after laser welding to meet imbalance and strength requirements</cite>.
- Cross-wedge rolling produces triaxial compressive stress states that improve microstructure and enable closer tolerances with less distortion; mandrel compensation controls ovality—beneficial for concentricity of rotor-hub interfaces.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Triaxial compressive stress improves microstructure; mandrel compensation resolves knifing-induced ovality</cite>.
- AM precision advances enable tight tolerances but often still require machining for surface integrity and dynamic balance in high-speed motors.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Advancing Precision in Additive Manufacturing proceedings document precision capabilities relevant to finishing for motor operation</cite>.

4.5 Residual Stress and Fatigue Considerations
- Forging and roll/press operations induce compressive residual stresses that improve fatigue; cross-wedge rolling’s triaxial compression is explicitly noted.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling produces triaxial compressive stress states, improving microstructure and potentially fatigue performance</cite>.
- Welding (laser) in modular shafts requires careful process control and post-weld machining to manage residual stress and imbalance; machining restores surface integrity and reduces eccentricity contributions to imbalance.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Laser welding of forged ends to tubular centers followed by fine machining addresses joint integrity and balance</cite>.
- AM introduces thermal cycles that can create residual stress; heat treatment and machining are used to mitigate and meet surface/balance specs.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Precision in AM emphasizes process control and finishing to manage residual effects for functional performance</cite>.

4.6 Scalability and Design Flexibility
- Forging + Machining: Scalable for high volumes; modular design reduces tooling and supports multiple power ratings by varying center-piece length, as in the electrified-truck case.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Different power ratings achieved by varying the length of the center piece; modular concept shared manufacturing processes and tooling</cite>.
- Extrusion/Rolling: Good for stepped hollow profiles; parameterizable process chains allow design tailoring; suitable for aluminum weight reduction programs.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Movable-sleeve extrusion parameter set (flange diameter, cavity height, chamfer angle) controlled stability and geometry; cross-wedge rolling produced stepped hollow sleeves with ovality control</cite>.
- Casting/AM: High design flexibility for internal cooling and hollow topologies; AM particularly valuable for complex internal features; costlier at scale.

5. Recommended Manufacturing Routes for NEV Electric Drive Units
5.1 Cost- and Volume-Oriented Routes
- Near-net forged end pieces + laser-welded hollow tubular center + CNC finishing: This hybrid modular route is highly suitable for NEV traction motors where high-speed strength, low imbalance, and cost-effective mass production are required. It leverages mature forging and welding technologies, minimizes waste via hollow tube centers, and uses modular design to share tooling and reduce development time, with quantified weight savings versus solid shafts.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">A three-part design with forged, pre-machined ends, laser-welded tubular center, and fine machining achieved up to 9 kg weight savings; modular concept reduced tooling and resource use</cite>.
- Extrusion or cross-wedge rolling of hollow stepped profiles + machining: For aluminum or steel tube semifinished products that match motor contours, these routes offer high material efficiency and good dimensional control, with rolling-induced compressive stresses aiding fatigue; ideal for weight-sensitive designs where machining can be standardized.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling with mandrel achieved near-stub-bar-free hollow stepped sleeves with controlled ovality and triaxial compressive stresses; sleeve-assisted extrusion of 6060 aluminum controlled underfill and flange geometry</cite>.

5.2 High-Performance/Complex-Geometry Routes
- AM of near-full-density hollow hubs/rotors with selective machining: Suitable for prototyping and limited-series NEV platforms needing complex internal cooling or integrated features, where AM provides rapid path to functional prototypes and tooling flexibility, but requires machining and heat treatment to meet surface/balance specs and fatigue margins.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Proceedings on precision in AM indicate capability to produce complex hollow geometries that are subsequently finished for high-speed operation</cite>.
- Investment/centrifugal casting of hollow rotors + machining: Appropriate for medium-lot production of thin-walled hollow rotors where casting yields good surface finish and near-net geometry, followed by precision machining and heat treatment to meet strength and balance targets, as implied by the modular shaft’s use of tubular centers and machining.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Tubular center plus fine machining to meet imbalance and surface constraints suggests casting/tube-derived hollow cores followed by machining</cite>.

5.3 Material-Specific Recommendations
- Steels (HSLA/maraging) for high-speed, high-load traction motors: Prefer forging + machining or roll/press-based near-net hollowing; hybrid modular designs for weight and cost; manage residual stress via controlled forging and post-weld machining.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Modular forged end pieces and tubular centers machined to meet high-speed strength and low-imbalance requirements</cite><cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling produces triaxial compressive stresses improving microstructure and aiding fatigue</cite>.
- Aluminum alloys for weight-sensitive motors: Use extrusion or rolling to near-net hollow profiles, then machining; sleeve-assisted extrusion methods can stabilize flange/underfill for reliable hollow contours; suitable where fatigue margins are adequate for alloy grade and surface finishes are maintained.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Sleeve-assisted extrusion of 6060 aluminum tubes demonstrated parameter-driven control of underfill and flange geometry</cite>.
- High-Ni alloys for high-temperature or high-sped regimes: AM or casting to create complex hollow geometries, followed by heat treatment/aging and machining for surface integrity and balance; justified by performance needs when weight or thermal limits drive material choice.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Precision in AM enables complex hollow geometries that can be finished for motor operation</cite>.

6. Implementation Guidance and Trade-offs
- Process integration: Combine near-net forming (forging/rolling/extrusion/casting) with precision machining and, where applicable, laser welding to restore surface integrity and balance; modularization reduces tooling and supports multi-variant platforms as in the electrified-truck case.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Modular rotor shafts combined forged, pre-machined ends with a tubular center, laser welded and then fine-machined; modular design reduced tooling and development time</cite>.
- Residual stress management: Favor processes that induce compressive triaxial stresses (cross-wedge rolling, controlled forging) and plan post-weld machining and stress-relief where welds exist; for AM, schedule heat treatment and machining to mitigate residual stress effects.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling produces triaxial compressive stress fields improving microstructure</cite><cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Fine machining after laser welding restores surface integrity and balance</cite><cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">AM precision practices address residual effects through finishing</cite>.
- Cost/performance frontier: For mainstream NEV traction motors, hybrid forging + tube center + machining offers the best balance of strength, imbalance, and cost; AM is advantageous for novelty/internal-cooling features and short runs; extrusion/rolling are attractive for aluminum weight reduction with standardized machining.

7. Conclusions and Evidence Gaps
- The most suitable manufacturing routes for hollow motor shafts in NEV electric drive units are: (1) near-net forged end pieces laser-welded to hollow tubular centers followed by CNC finishing; (2) extrusion or cross-wedge rolling of hollow stepped profiles followed by machining; and (3) AM of complex hollow geometries with subsequent heat treatment and machining for high-performance/complex-geometry variants.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">A modular forged and machined rotor shaft achieved weight savings and shared manufacturing processes</cite><cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling and sleeve-assisted extrusion produce controlled hollow stepped profiles with efficient material use and favorable microstructure</cite><cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">AM precision advancements enable complex hollow geometries that are finished for motor operation</cite>.
- Open gaps include head-to-head cost and lead-time data across scales for aluminum versus steel hollow shafts in production motors and detailed residual stress mapping for welded modular joints; targeted benchmarking and pilot builds are recommended to finalize process chains for specific NEV platforms.

Appendix: Summary Table of Forming Techniques
- Solid billet forging + machining hollow: Mature, high-throughput; requires machining; suitable for steels and aluminum; residual compressive stresses favorable.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Forged end pieces pre-machined and fine-machined to meet strength and imbalance</cite>.
- Extrusion (tube) + machining: Controlled hollow flanges/underfill; parameter-tunable; good for aluminum weight reduction; near-net material efficiency.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Movable-sleeve extrusion of 6060 tubes controlled underfill and flange geometry</cite>.
- Cross-wedge rolling (hollow stepped) + machining: Near-stub-bar-free; ovality control via mandrel; triaxial compressive stresses; efficient production of stepped hollow shafts.<cite id="call_e2076a81cb6f-0">Cross-wedge rolling with mandrel controlled axial movement and ovality; triaxial compression improves microstructure</cite>.
- Investment/centrifugal casting + machining: Near-net hollow cores; good surface finish; machining and heat treatment required; medium-lot flexibility.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Tubular center plus fine machining indicates casting/tube-derived hollow cores followed by machining</cite>.
- Additive manufacturing (near-full density hollow) + machining: Rapid complex hollow geometries; high material/energy cost; machining and heat treatment for properties and balance.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-1">Precision in AM enables complex hollow geometries that are finished for motor operation</cite>.
- Hybrid modular forging + laser welding + machining: Combines forging efficiency and hollow center benefits; modular scaling; post-weld machining critical for imbalance control.<cite id="call_4a87e8753f27-0">Forged ends laser-welded to tubular center and fine-machined; modular design reduced tooling and achieved up to 9 kg weight savings</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Are AI fashion design tools leading to creative homogenization? Governance and dispute resolution for independent designers vs. algorithms

Executive summary
- AI fashion design tools are increasingly embedded in brand workflows, enabling rapid generation of garment images and layouts but often trained on curated corpora of trending designs, which pushes outputs toward statistical averages of current styles and risks convergence across brands using similar tools and prompts.<cite id="call_08c9105072fb-0">With the recent expansion of the applicability of the AI into the creative realm, attempts are being made to use AI in the garment development system in various ways, both in academia and the fashion business; several IT companies have developed and possess AI-based garment design technologies that utilize StyleGAN2 for image transformation, though adoption is not yet widespread</cite><cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Most AI fashion tools work the same way: they train on millions of trending images from Instagram, Pinterest, and fashion websites; asking for a “summer dress” returns the algorithm’s statistical average, so brands using the same tool get nearly identical outputs</cite>. 
- Evidence from co-creative studies shows meaningful alignment between AI proposals and human designers at category level, suggesting shared stylistic tendencies that can amplify uniformity when brands standardize prompts and review processes.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">When evaluated on 30 T-shirt illustrations, Gemini’s layout proposals matched actual products in 12/30 strict cases but 20/30 at grouped category level; matches with five professional designers ranged from 18–24/30, indicating a level of commonality with human decisions</cite>.
- Copyright disputes center on training on protected/pre-existing designs, originality thresholds for AI-generated outputs, and ownership/indemnity in AI-assisted works. Legal analyses across UK/EU/US warn that scraping and unlicensed use can infringe reproduction rights and that AI-assisted outputs may still meet originality if sufficiently transformed, but policy proposals increasingly favor making AI-generated fashion works copyrightable and owned by the deploying designer, with clear licensing and provenance safeguards.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Use of in-copyright fashion designs in training corpora raises infringement risks; under UK/EU law, AI-assisted designs can still be original applied art, and AI-generated derivatives implicate reproduction and transformative use doctrines</cite><cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-1">AI tools create fabric designs and clothing and raise ownership questions; policy proposals recommend that AI-generated and AI-assisted designs be copyrightable and owned by the designer who purchases/uses the AI device</cite>.

What AI fashion design tools do and how they shape aesthetics
- Contemporary AI garment design systems use generative networks (e.g., StyleGAN2) to transform images and propose designs, integrating into garment development workflows to boost efficiency; however, real-world adoption remains limited and calls for domain-aware systems that respect fashion processes.<cite id="call_08c9105072fb-0">AI-based garment design tools using StyleGAN2 exist and can increase efficiency for the many designs needed per season, but are not widely utilized; research aims to analyze and integrate with human garment development processes</cite>. 
- Co-creative evaluations show that generative systems can propose layout variants that human designers recognize as reasonable, especially when categories are grouped, indicating that AI proposals cluster around common design archetypes that brands then curate into collections.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Gemini’s T-shirt layout explanations were deemed “reasonable” by over half of illustrators, and matches to designers’ choices were 18–24 out of 30 at grouped category level</cite>.
- Market-facing tools emphasize speed and brand consistency: brands report accelerating development from multi-week cycles to days while maintaining a consistent visual language, which can lock in homogenized palettes and motifs when powered by shared datasets and prompt libraries.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-2">Fashion brands are revolutionizing design process with AI, reducing development time from six weeks to days while maintaining brand consistency</cite>.

Mechanisms of creative homogenization
- Training data echo chambers: Tools trained on scraped Instagram/Pinterest and fashion websites learn the statistical “average” of current styles; repeated prompts (e.g., “summer dress”) surface similar variants, and multiple brands using the same tool converge toward that average.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Most AI fashion tools train on millions of trending images from Instagram, Pinterest, and fashion websites; a “summer dress” prompt yields the algorithm’s statistical average, producing nearly identical outputs across brands using the same tool</cite>.
- Workflow amplification: Brands standardize prompts, style references, and approval workflows, which filter outputs toward safe, familiar archetypes; efficiency pressures further reward outputs that match known brand aesthetics over novel deviations.<cite id="call_08c9105072fb-0">Brands need numerous designs per season; AI-based generation can increase efficiency, but current tools are not widely utilized, motivating systems that incorporate fashion domain knowledge</cite><cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-2">AI accelerates development while maintaining brand consistency</cite>.
- Evidence of alignment: Empirical comparisons show AI proposals align with human designers at higher-level category groupings, indicating shared stylistic norms that can be amplified into collections and across teams.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Grouped category matches between Gemini and designers ranged from 18–24/30, evidencing commonality</cite>.

Indicators and measurement
- Design taxonomy similarity: Compare AI-generated and human-crafted garment images/layouts at sub- and broad-category levels to quantify convergence across collections and seasons.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Strict vs. grouped category matching shows how much AI proposals align with actual products and professional designers</cite>.
- Brand aesthetic distance: Track pairwise similarity of seasonal palettes, silhouettes, and motifs across brands using the same or similar tools; declines in diversity indices signal homogenization.
- Reuse and derivative density: Monitor reuse of AI-generated assets across brands and collections; high reuse without substantial transformation suggests derivative convergence.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">AI-generated derivatives implicate reproduction and transformative use; training on pre-existing designs raises infringement risks</cite>.

Copyright risks and the current legal landscape
- Training on protected works: Using in-copyright designs (e.g., runway looks, prints, CAD renderings) without consent can infringe reproduction rights; outputs may copy protected expression, especially if prompts and reference images are tightly coupled to specific works.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">In-copyright pre-existing designs can be part of the corpus mined for training gen-AI; use in new design creation can negate originality and raise infringement under InfoSoc and CDPA, while AI-assisted outputs can still be original applied art</cite>.
- Originality and ownership: UK/EU analyses suggest AI-assisted designs can retain originality if they reflect the creator’s own selection, coordination, and artistic choices; AI-generated outputs may not be protected as “art,” but transformative derivatives can be, depending on authorship and fixation. US-focused proposals argue for making AI-generated and AI-assisted fashion works copyrightable and owned by the deploying designer to protect investment and deter scraping.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">AI-assisted designs can derive from diverse archives and still be novel; CJEU decisions and Infoepa inform originality assessments</cite><cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-1">Policy proposals recommend that AI-generated and AI-assisted designs be copyrightable and owned by the designer who purchases/uses the AI device</cite>.
- Orphan works and scraping: When training data include unattributed designer works, platforms and brands may face contributory or vicarious liability if they profit from derivative outputs or facilitate access; legal uncertainty persists across jurisdictions as courts and regulators catch up.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Mining in-copyright design corpora raises infringement risks under reproduction rights and derivative works doctrines</cite>.

How disputes between independent designers and algorithms can be resolved
1) Licensing and data-use agreements
- Clear licenses for training and inference: Use CC0 or similar waivers from the designer’s archives to avoid reproduction claims; include opt-in clauses for scraping, image extraction, and embedding, with attribution and audit rights.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Enriching AI systems with diverse archives can foster innovation, but requires lawful text-and-data mining practices</cite>.
- Platform/vendor contracts: Require AI vendors to license datasets used for training on third-party works; indemnify licensors against claims from scraping or unauthorized derivatives; mandate removal of outputs upon cease-and-desist.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Use of AI tools in new design creation can negate originality and infringe reproduction rights, underscoring the need for licensor protections</cite>.
- Derivative carve-outs: Pay secondary licenses for AI-generated derivatives that incorporate protected elements; set royalty rates proportional to exposure and similarity metrics (e.g., motif reuse).

2) Provenance, watermarks, and audit trails
- Digital provenance tags: Embed metadata in AI-generated garment images and files recording dataset sources, prompts, reference images, and transformations; enable automated similarity audits across collections.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">AI outputs reflect the statistical average of training images; provenance can expose data lineage and prompt histories</cite>.
- Watermarking and perceptual hashes: Apply imperceptible watermarks to AI outputs and compute perceptual hashes for prints and renderings to detect unlicensed reproduction; integrate with brand compliance tools.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Transformative use and reproduction rights interact; watermarking and metadata can support rights management and enforcement</cite>.

3) Governance and co-creation guardrails
- Prompt and reference-image audits: Require designers to disclose top-5 reference images and prompt tokens for AI proposals; human curators approve variants that exceed similarity thresholds to known originals.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Gemini’s explanations were deemed reasonable by illustrators, suggesting explainability can support collaborative design with oversight</cite>.
- Diversity quotas: Enforce minimum diversity constraints (e.g., categorical spread across silhouette, fabric, color, motif) and randomize seed variants to counteract echo chambers.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Grouped category matches show commonality; diversifying prompts and selection can reduce convergence</cite>.
- Intermediary safe harbors: Platform policies adopt AI-content review for fashion design uploads, takedown on notice, and limited liability if the platform can show it “does not have actual knowledge” of infringement and acts expeditiously on notice, mirroring DMCA/takedown regimes.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Reproduction and derivative work doctrines motivate platforms to implement notice-and-takedown and access controls</cite>.

4) Dispute resolution pathways
- Mediation/arbitration: Embedding mandatory IP mediation clauses for AI-assisted design disputes; neutral fashion IP experts assess similarity and originality and recommend remedies (takedown, credit, licensing terms).<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-1">Policy proposals recommend clear ownership and rights for AI-assisted designs to reduce litigation and align incentives</cite>.
- Standards and certifications: Create “Ethical AI Fashion” seals requiring provenance, license coverage, and diversity metrics; regulators can audit brands and penalize scraping or unlicensed training.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Diverse archives can drive innovation; legal clarity on text-and-data mining and originality supports certification</cite>.
- Collective licensing: Unions and indie designer collectives license non-exclusive rights to train on anonymized, aggregated datasets, sharing royalties across members to monetize exposure while enabling safer generative pipelines.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Mining diverse archives can contribute to novel original works if done within legal frameworks</cite>.

Practical steps for brands and independent designers
- For brands: 
  - Conduct dataset audits; require vendors to disclose training sources and indemnify for scraping-related claims.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Use of in-copyright designs in training can negate originality and infringe reproduction rights</cite>.
  - Implement provenance capture and automated similarity scans before production drops.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">AI outputs reflect statistical averages of training data; provenance and oversight can mitigate convergence</cite>.
  - Diversify engines and prompts; enforce category-level diversity quotas to avoid stylistic lock-in.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Grouped category alignment suggests commonality; diversification reduces identical outputs</cite>.
- For independent designers:
  - License your work under CC0-with-attribution for non-commercial AI training, or negotiate paid derivative licenses specifying usage scopes and audit rights.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Mining in-copyright corpora raises infringement risks; clear licensing enables lawful use</cite>.
  - Watermark digital assets; use takedown notices and mediation to address unauthorized AI derivatives.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Reproduction and transformative use doctrines support notice-and-takedown strategies</cite>.

Limitations and outlook
- Evidence on large-scale homogenization is still emerging; most quantitative studies focus on co-creative alignment rather than market-wide aesthetic convergence. Future work should deploy style embeddings and motif similarity indices across seasons and brands to quantify diversity loss and track interventions.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Empirical studies show partial alignment and reasonable explanations, but broader market-level uniformity requires systematic measurement</cite>.
- Jurisdictions differ on originality thresholds and liability for AI outputs; harmonization efforts (EU directive proposals, US policy) and industry standards will reduce uncertainty and make licensing more predictable.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">UK/EU analyses frame originality and infringement; policy evolution will clarify rights</cite><cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-1">US policy proposals advocate for designer ownership of AI-assisted works</cite>.

Appendix: Key references and data points
- AI garment design workflow and efficiency potential; limited but growing adoption of StyleGAN2-based tools in industry.<cite id="call_08c9105072fb-0">AI-based garment design tools using StyleGAN2 exist; brands need many designs per season; adoption is limited but efficiency gains are plausible</cite>.
- Co-creative alignment evidence (T-shirt layouts) showing 18–24/30 matches with professional designers at grouped categories; explainability supports collaboration.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-0">Gemini proposals matched actual products in 12/30 strict cases, 20/30 at grouped level; matches with designers 18–24/30; illustrators found explanations reasonable</cite>.
- Industry acceleration of development cycles while maintaining brand consistency.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-2">Brands reduce development time from six weeks to days while maintaining brand consistency</cite>.
- Market growth and investment in AI fashion design applications (trend forecasting, visual content, pattern/textile) underscoring urgency for governance.<cite id="call_bebb4f2c8b99-4">Adoption rates: trend forecasting 72%, visual content creation 69%, pattern & textile design 65%, with over $1.2B investment</cite>.
- Legal analyses and policy proposals on originality, reproduction rights, and ownership for AI-assisted and AI-generated fashion works.<cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-0">Copyright implications of training on pre-existing designs; AI-assisted designs can retain originality; infringement risks under InfoSoc/CDPA</cite><cite id="call_b45371e1df3f-1">Policy proposals: AI-generated and AI-assisted designs should be copyrightable and owned by the deploying designer</cite>.

</answer>

In light of both UK and EU copyright law, the article analyses the circumstances under which the use of AI tools in new design creation can negate their originality as works of applied art under Infoepa and subsequent CJEU decisions, whilst enriching the discussion with elements of fashion theory. It further examines copyright infringement concerning AI-generated fashion design outputs, focusing on the right of reproduction under the InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC and the UK CDPA 1988, as well as transformative uses of AI-generated derivative designs. The article concludes that gen-AI can have a considerable impact for fostering fashion innovation. An AI device’s ability to generate fashion designs raises the question of who will own the copyrights of the fashion designs. Title: How Netflix adapted One Hundred Years of Solitude: strategies, production, and reception

Summary
Netflix’s adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude launched in two parts on the streaming platform, with the first eight episodes released Dec 11, 2024 and production for the second and final part beginning in February 2025; Netflix announced the second season would premiere in August 2026, closing the audiovisual cycle of the novel’s Macondo epic. The series was filmed entirely in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors, and was undertaken with the support and specific requests of García Márquez’s family. Directors Alex García López and Laura Mora framed the project as a poetic reimagining of magical realism, restructured the novel’s nonlinearity for dramatic coherence, and emphasized long, location-based takes and theatrical set design. Critics and early audience metrics suggest strong reception, though the adaptation’s “success” is still unfolding as Part 2 arrives.

1. What Netflix adapted and when
- Netflix acquired and executed a limited-series adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude, premiering the first part on December 11, 2024 in eight episodes, with a second part of eight episodes released in two batches across 2026 after production in 2025. <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-0">The series will run for 16 episodes on Netflix, with the first eight released on 11 December 2024</cite> <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-1">the second and final season of the series One Hundred Years of Solitude will premiere in August 2026</cite> <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-3">Production for the second installment began February 11, 2025</cite>.
- The project was explicitly Colombia-based: the family requested filming in Colombia, with Colombian actors in Spanish; producers scouted locations including Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, and Barranquilla. <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-0">The series will run for 16 episodes on Netflix, with the first eight released on 11 December 2024</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors; producers scouted locations including Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, and Barranquilla</cite>.
- Netflix framed the adaptation as an “ambitious” and “monumental” screen cycle of García Márquez’s masterpiece, timed to the centennial of the author’s life. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-2">Netflix unveiled an ambitious adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s “Cent ans de solitude” in December 2024</cite>.

2. Creative and structural strategies
- Directors García López and Laura Mora set out to reinterpret magical realism not as “fantasy” but as a poetic extension of everyday Latin American reality, using long, wandering location shots and handcrafted, theatrical sets to create a sense of place. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-0">One great gamble was to distance magical realism from a fantastic frame and embrace it as a poetic place; shot on location in Colombia with long wandering shots and a handcrafted, theatrical sensibility</cite>.
- The series restructures the novel’s nonlinearity for screen clarity while preserving its dreamlike temporality: writers organized chronologically to resolve inconsistencies for dramatic coherence and expanded on the book’s implied, often summarized scenes into scenes and conversations. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-4">They didn’t alter written scenes; they organized the non-linear narrative chronologically to resolve inconsistencies for dramatic coherence and expanded implied moments into scenes and conversations</cite>.
- The creative team emphasized fidelity to García Márquez’s cultural and linguistic world, resisting Hollywood tropes: “as a Colombian, it has been an honor and an… obligation to tell this story,” and “the García Márquez family insisted on Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors.” <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">The family requested filming in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors</cite> <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-2">“It was incredibly important to the García Márquez family that it had to be filmed in Colombia, with Colombian actors in Spanish,” says García López</cite>.
- Critics note that the show’s approach privileges a quiet, “不动声色” realism where the extraordinary is treated as everyday, aligning with the novel’s “impossible things as commonplace” style. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-1">Directors aimed to “reproduce as fully as possible the reality” of the novel, letting characters “unmovedly” experience a magic that is “taken for granted,” matching Maupassant’s maxim</cite>.

3. Production commitments: locations, scale, and authenticity
- Filming took place across multiple Colombian locales to anchor Macondo in lived geography: Cali (rainforest), Villavicencio (Magdalena River delta), Girardot and Palomino (near Bogotá), Santa Marta (north coast), and Barranquilla (Caribbean port). <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">Producers scouted Cali, Villavicencio, Girardot, Palomino, Santa Marta, and Barranquilla</cite>.
- The production design and cinematography favor long takes and physical continuity, aiming for a “theatrical” craft that allows characters to move through spaces rather than relying on heavy VFX. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-0">Long wandering shots and a handcrafted, theatrical sensibility</cite>.
- The team explicitly positioned the adaptation as Colombia’s story for the world, with a national cast and crew, to honor the novel’s roots in Colombian history and landscape. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-2">“It was incredibly important to the García Márquez family that it had to be filmed in Colombia, with Colombian actors in Spanish,” says García López</cite>.

4. Archival and estate considerations
- The project was undertaken with the support and guidance of García Márquez’s family, who were directly involved in creative and production decisions (e.g., language, casting, country). <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez’s family, who requested Colombia, Spanish, and Colombian actors</cite>.
- Some summaries describe the series as “authorized,” with executive producers including García Márquez’s sons; Netflix has commemorated centennial milestones with programming and publicity around the work. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-1">In 2024, the book was adapted into an authorized television series released on Netflix and executive produced by García Márquez’s sons</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-4">On October 21, 2022, Netflix commemorated the for… [the centennial], and in 2024 adapted it into an authorized series</cite>.
- Broader archival efforts around García Márquez’s papers have been expanding globally (e.g., University of Texas digitizing 27,000 pages), which Netflix could leverage for authenticity and promotion, though this series’ materials are not yet cataloged in those repositories. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">The University of Texas opened a large online archive of Marquez materials (27,000 pages) in Spanish and English</cite>.

5. Distribution, marketing, and audience reception
- Netflix marketed the series as a “monumental” or “ambitious” adaptation, timed to the centennial, and previewed episodes via its Tudum platform; the first part launched Dec 11, 2024, with a two-part, 16-episode structure. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-2">Netflix announced the adaptation as “monumental,” premiering Dec 2024</cite> <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-2">There will be 16 episodes in two parts of eight each, with the first part on Dec 11, 2024</cite> <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-0">The series will run for 16 episodes on Netflix, with the first eight released on 11 December 2024</cite>.
- Early audience-signal aggregators list strong scores: IMDb ~8.4, Lostfilm ~8.3, suggesting positive reception among viewers, though professional critical consensus is still consolidating as Part 2 releases. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">Lostfilm lists 8.3; IMDb shows 8.4 for the series</cite>.
- Critics emphasize the show’s “daunting task” and its commitment to cultural specificity, which Netflix highlighted in previews and creator interviews. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-2">García López calls it a “daunting task,” underscoring the cultural weight</cite>.

6. How this differs from earlier attempts
- Previous efforts struggled with either over-fantastical or Hollywoodized depictions of magical realism, long-form fidelity, and casting/setting. Netflix countered by grounding Macondo in Colombia’s real places, insisting on Spanish with Colombian actors, and treating magical realism as poetic realism to be staged rather than “fantastic.” <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-0">Embracing magical realism as poetic rather than fantastic, shot on location with long takes and theatrical sets</cite> <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-2">Family-driven Colombia, Spanish, and Colombian actors</cite>.
- The series also tackled the novel’s extreme nonlinearity by resequencing for coherence while preserving the “dreamlike” texture through expanded implied scenes—something earlier adaptations often glossed or fragmented. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-4">Organizing non-linear narrative chronologically and expanding implied moments into scenes</cite>.

7. What “success” looks like
- Netflix’s definition of success includes global reach, completion of the two-part cycle, and positive audience metrics; cultural/estate alignment and Colombia-centric production broaden its legitimacy as a “world” adaptation. Early data (two-part release plan, strong audience scores) point in that direction, with final verdicts still pending as Part 2 arrives in 2026. <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-1">Second season announced for August 2026, closing the adaptation cycle</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">Lostfilm 8.3 and IMDb 8.4 suggest strong early audience reception</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-1">Authorized series executive-produced by García Márquez’s sons</cite>.

8. Key takeaways for Netflix’s approach
- Treat the novel as a cultural epic of Colombia, not just a fantasy novel: anchor language, actors, and locations in Colombia to build authenticity. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-2">Colombian filming, Spanish, Colombian actors per family request</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">Scouted multiple Colombian locations</cite>.
- Reimagine magical realism poetically on camera: favor long, physical takes and theatrical design over heavy FX, and stage the “impossible” as everyday. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-0">Long wandering shots and theatrical craft; magical realism as poetic</cite> <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-1">Quiet, “taken-for-granted” magic aligns with the novel’s style</cite>.
- Manage nonlinearity as structural drama: resequence chronologically for clarity but keep the dreamlike texture by expanding implied scenes into grounded conversations and actions. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-4">Chronological restructuring and expansion of implied moments</cite>.
- Build legitimacy via estate and archival alignment: work with García Márquez’s family and leverage expanding global archives to ensure cultural fidelity. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-1">Authorized series executive-produced by García Márquez’s sons</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">Global digitization of Marquez papers (UT) supports broader authenticity</cite>.

Remaining uncertainties and what to watch
- Budgetary figures, full cast/character mapping across generations, and deeper archival citations (e.g., specific Manuscrito materials used) are not yet widely documented in public sources; Netflix’s full credits and behind-the-scenes supplements will likely clarify production scale and specific archival uses. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-1">Some sources describe the series as “authorized” with family involvement</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">University of Texas archive provides broader context but is separate from Netflix’s production records</cite>.
- Critical consensus will solidify after Part 2 releases; early audience scores are promising but not definitive. <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">IMDb ~8.4, Lostfilm ~8.3 indicate strong early reception</cite> <cite id="call_ec5b41ad2e0d-1">Part 2 release in August 2026 will complete the cycle</cite>.

Bottom line
Netflix “managed” the adaptation by repositioning One Hundred Years of Solitude as a Colombian epic told in Macondo’s real geography and language, staging magical realism as poetic realism, restructuring the novel’s nonlinearity for screen while preserving its dreamlike texture, and aligning closely with García Márquez’s family and cultural legacy. The two-part release model, Colombia-first production, and early positive audience signals suggest a credible, data-driven path to “success” for a notoriously difficult book to translate to screen. <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-0">Embracing magical realism poetically with long, location-based takes and theatrical craft</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-3">Colombia-only filming, Spanish, Colombian actors, and multi-city locations</cite> <cite id="call_9da2587311f5-4">Managing nonlinearity and expanding implied scenes</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-1">Family authorization and executive production by García Márquez’s sons</cite> <cite id="call_4ed35df08281-0">Early audience scores (IMDb ~8.4, Lostfilm ~8.3) and expanding archives contextualize authenticity</cite>.
</answer>
