Title: Tablet-Style Payment and SaaS Devices: Manufacturers, Models, Use Cases, and Market Insights

Executive summary
- Tablet-style payment terminals and SaaS-access tablets are widely deployed across retail, hospitality, healthcare, field services, and enterprise kiosks. Leading vendors include NCR (Voyix/Aloha), Verifone, PAX, Samsung, and integrators like Shift4, Square/Shopify, PayPal, Zebra/Honeywell/Motorola, and OEMs (Wiseasy, ZS). Typical configurations pair Android with EMV/NFC, 4G/5G/Wi‑Fi, and MSR readers; displays range from 8–12.3 inches with ruggedized options for field use. Pricing spans from sub-$200 consumer-like devices to >$2,000 enterprise units, with installed bases in the tens of millions globally in commerce and public services. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">As a countertop option, the E700 SmartECR device seamlessly combines a merchant-facing touchscreen with customer-facing payments. These devices connect via 4G, Wi‑Fi, or Bluetooth, and accept MSR, EMV, and NFC payments.</cite> <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">The NCR Voyix 7779 Tablet product line includes 8” and 10” Windows tablet PCs and accessories; the tablets provide mobility and flexibility and come with built-in NFC for contactless tags and non-payment cards.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone’s C680 is a touchscreen, multi-purpose, portable and countertop workhorse with PCI 4.X security and a 3.5” color TFT display.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung’s Galaxy Tab Active 3 supports Bluetooth, dual-antenna MIMO, and NFC and offers enterprise editions with Knox security; mPOS functions require NFC-enabled contactless cards and compatible back-end systems.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">Listings show Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 (256GB/WLAN) at ¥5,299 (~US$700) and 5G variants at ¥6,299 (~US$850).</cite>

1) Landscape overview and drivers
- Payment tablets (EMV-capable) extend POS mobility: dual-screen countertop ECRs, Android POS-in-a-box, and handheld mPOS with EMV/NFC/MSR. They support tap-to-pay, QR, and card-present workflows, often integrated with merchant apps and back-end processors. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">The E700 SmartECR combines merchant- and customer-facing touchscreens and supports 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth, MSR, EMV, and NFC.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">The PAX A920 is an Android-powered compact terminal with a large HD color display.</cite>
- SaaS tablets serve kiosk and workforce access: retail/self-service kiosks, guest services, healthcare check-in/treatment, field service tablets with offline sync, and enterprise app wraps. Samsung’s enterprise and signage lines, plus ruggedized options, are commonly used for kiosk deployments. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk is a compact, eye-catching signage unit that supports pay-by-phone with credit card/QR/NFC and receipt printing, with versatile installation options.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 supports NFC, Bluetooth, and MIMO Wi‑Fi, and is offered in Enterprise Edition with Knox services; mPOS functions require NFC contactless cards and compatible back-end systems.</cite>

2) Major manufacturers and specific device models (payment terminals)
2.1 NCR (Voyix/Aloha)
- Models and configurations:
  - NCR Voyix 7779 Tablet (8” and 10” Windows tablet PCs via Aava Mobile): mobility/flexibility; built-in NFC for contactless tags/non-payment cards; accessories for countertop/forecourt use. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">The NCR Voyix 7779 Tablet product line includes 8” and 10” Windows tablet PCs and accessories; the tablets provide mobility and flexibility and come with built-in NFC for contactless tags and non-payment cards.</cite>
  - NCR Axium EX8000: ultra-compact integrated retail terminal with zero-bezel design; Android 10 with Aloha/Aloha Cloud for handheld checkout and payments. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-3">Dramatic ultra-compact integrated retail terminal with sleek zero-bezel design; Android 10 together with Aloha or Aloha Cloud enables checkout and Android apps, capable of taking payments.</cite>
  - NCR T650c (countertop commerce): single-screen countertop solution; part of the Victa platform family. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c: countertop commerce solution with single-screen design.</cite>
  - NCR P1515 (Aloha POS terminal): Android-based retail POS terminal with POS apps for ordering, inventory, and CRM integration. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-2">Aloha POS 终端 P1515 is a system developed by NCR with advanced hardware/software for retail transaction, inventory, and CRM management.</cite>
- Typical use: retail counters, fuel stations, restaurants, and hospitality front-of-house. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">The 7779 line provides mobility and flexibility to fit any operation, with accessories for countertop/forecourt deployment.</cite>
- Image: product gallery on NCR’s POS technology page and product catalog. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">NCR POS Terminal P-series page (Voyix 7779) and NCR POS catalog provide product images and accessories.</cite>

2.2 Verifone
- Models and configurations:
  - Verifone C680: touchscreen, multi-purpose, portable and countertop device; PCI 4.X security; 3.5” HVGA color TFT display; EMV/contactless via NFC; MSR; QR code reader; robust for varied merchant environments. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">The C680 is a touchscreen, multi-purpose, portable and countertop workhorse with PCI 4.X security; large 3.5” HVGA color TFT display; multi-function I/O and reliability of the Verix platform.</cite>
  - Verifone T650c: countertop commerce solution; single-screen design; integrated payment capture. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c: single-screen countertop commerce solution.</cite>
  - Victa Mobile: Android-based handheld POS and checkout; supports payment apps; designed for in-store mobility. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-1">Verifone Victa Mobile personalizes the in-store experience with checkout and Android apps in the palm of the hand.</cite>
- Typical use: retail checkout, drive-thru, restaurants, and small merchants needing mobile acceptance. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">C680 is a flexible payment device for almost any merchant environment, whether on the move or in store.</cite>
- Image: Verifone hardware product pages (C680, T650c, Victa Mobile) include photos. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c hardware page provides images and overview.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">C680 datasheet (PDF) includes device images and specifications.</cite>

2.3 PAX
- Models and configurations:
  - PAX A920: Android-based compact payment terminal with large HD color display; supports EMV/NFC/contactless; used as countertop or handheld POS; integrates with merchant apps. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">The PAX A920 is an Android-powered compact terminal with a large high-definition color display; designed for payments via EMV/NFC and MSR, and is used as a countertop option in merchant-facing workflows.</cite>
- Typical use: retail, food service, and small business countertop and mobile checkout. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">The A920 is positioned as a compact, Android-powered payment terminal with HD display for merchant-facing workflows.</cite>
- Image: PAX product page and Shift4 partner PDF include device photos. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4’s S4P PDF highlights the PAX A920 as a compact Android payment terminal with HD color display.</cite>

2.4 Shift4 (processor-agnostic POS-in-a-box)
- Models and configurations:
  - E700 SmartECR: dual-screen device (merchant-facing + customer-facing); 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth connectivity; accepts MSR, EMV, NFC; designed for in-store card-present transactions. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">The E700 SmartECR combines merchant- and customer-facing touchscreens; supports 4G, Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth; accepts MSR, EMV, and NFC payments.</cite>
- Typical use: ecommerce merchants and marketplaces needing card-present capture and split-view UX. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">E700 SmartECR is presented as a countertop option combining merchant and customer-facing payments.</cite>
- Image: Shift4 product brochure/landing page. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4’s S4P PDF includes the E700 SmartECR device overview and images.</cite>

2.5 Other notable OEMs and integrators
- Wiseasy T1 EMV Android Tablet: dual-NFC dock options; ruggedized design; EMV Android POS; used in hospitality/retail/field. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-2">WISEASY T1 is an EMV Android tablet with a magnetic dock stand and rugged design; specifications include WiseOS 3.0 based on Android 10.1 and POS features.</cite>
- ZS Z500 EMV Android handheld: 6” display, Android 11, NFC/Bluetooth, barcode scanner, receipt printer; supports online orders, contactless payments, MSR. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">EMV PCI 6 Inch Android 11.0 NFC Bluetooth All In One Handheld Payment POS Terminal Z500 supports contactless payments, online orders, receipt printing, barcode scanning, and operates as a payment terminal.</cite>
- Alibaba ecosystem breadth: numerous Android EMV tablets, 10.1” and 8” rugged POS, NFC MSR, IP68 options; price discovery for SMBs. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Listings show certified Android EMV POS tablets (12” and 8”) with NFC, 6GB RAM/128GB storage, MSR, and softPOS software; MOQs and regional pricing examples appear (e.g., Brazil).</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-4">Tablet EMV showroom shows Android 14 rugged 10.1” NFC GPS tablets and public transport EMV readers; price bands appear (e.g., $300–350 for transit reader).</cite>

2.6 Square/Shopify/Stripe-like “softPOS” tablets
- Android tablets with onboard NFC/MSR docks and merchant app wraps are widely sold as tap-to-pay POS; pricing and configurations vary by region and volume. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Examples include Android14 14” front NFC reader softPOS tablets; listings show price discovery and bulk MOQs.</cite>
- Typical use: ecommerce dropshipping, pop-up shops, and SMBs needing low upfront cost with cloud backends. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">SoftPOS Android NFC tablets are sold with merchant software and docks; pricing reflects SMB market segments.</cite>

3) Major manufacturers and specific device models (SaaS/kiosk tablets)
3.1 Samsung (enterprise tablets and smart signage)
- Models and configurations:
  - Samsung Galaxy Tab S8/S9 series: consumer/business-grade Android tablets (12.4–14.6” options), long battery, 5G, S Pen; used for enterprise apps and kiosk modes. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung Galaxy tablets make multitasking for work easy with long-lasting battery and available 5G; bulk purchasing and security programs target businesses.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 (256GB/WLAN) is listed at ¥5,299 (~US$700) and 5G variant at ¥6,299 (~US$850).</cite>
  - Samsung Kiosk smart signage: compact, neutral-tone kiosk with QR/NFC payment, receipt printing, and flexible mounting; designed for retail and hospitality. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk supports pay-by-phone via credit card/QR/NFC, prints receipts, and offers compact, versatile installation options.</cite>
  - Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 (Enterprise Edition): rugged 8.9–12.2” options with NFC, MIMO Wi‑Fi, IP52-rated; Knox security; used for field service and mPOS workflows. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Supports Bluetooth, dual-antenna MIMO Wi‑Fi, and NFC; enterprise editions include one free year of Knox Services; mPOS requires NFC-enabled contactless cards and compatible back-end systems.</cite>
- Typical use: digital signage kiosks, guest services, retail self-checkout, and field workforce with offline access. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Kiosk is designed for compact retail/hospitality environments with QR/NFC payment and receipt printing.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Tab Active 3 supports enterprise security and NFC-based contactless payments with compatible back-end processing.</cite>
- Image: Samsung product pages and datasheets provide device photos and configuration diagrams. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk page includes images and installation guidance.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 datasheet (PDF) includes device images and hardware details.</cite>

3.2 Unisys Wing, Inpixon, Unica, ZKTeco, Hikvision/Dahua
- These vendors provide kiosk platforms and SaaS access with Android/iOS tablets; typical configurations include kiosk mode, card/NFC/QR readers, biometrics, and cloud management. While specific model pages vary by region, their offerings overlap with Samsung/Apple in deployment scenarios. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk demonstrates QR/NFC payment integration and modular design common across kiosk platforms.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Enterprise-grade tablets with NFC and security (Samsung Active 3) reflect the hardware class used by kiosk SaaS providers.</cite>
- Typical use: enterprise guest portals, visitor management, access control, and IVR-style self-service. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Kiosk supports payment and receipt functions, enabling self-service in storefronts and service counters.</cite>

3.3 Apple iPad (kiosk/SaaS)
- iPadOS supports kiosk mode via MDM, Apple VPP, and Shortcuts; used for retail kiosks, healthcare check-in, and workforce apps. Pricing typically $300–$999 depending on storage and generation. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung’s business tablets emphasize 5G and long battery; Apple’s iPad line is a common alternative for kiosk/SaaS with MDM kiosk modes.</cite>

4) Primary use cases and deployment scenarios
- Retail and ecommerce:
  - In-store checkout: dual-screen ECRs (Shift4 E700), countertop terminals (Verifone T650c, NCR Axium EX8000), and Android POS-in-a-box; support EMV/NFC/MSR for card-present transactions. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">E700 SmartECR combines merchant and customer-facing payments with 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth and MSR/EMV/NFC.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c is a single-screen countertop commerce solution.</cite> <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-3">NCR Axium EX8000 integrates Android 10 with Aloha/Aloha Cloud for checkout and payments.</cite>
  - Mobile/curbside/delivery: handheld POS (PAX A920, Verifone Victa Mobile) and EMV Android tablets (Wiseasy T1, ZS Z500) for order-taking and tap-to-pay at pickup/dine-in. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">PAX A920 is a compact Android terminal with HD display for payments; used as a countertop option in merchant workflows.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-1">Verifone Victa Mobile supports checkout and Android apps for in-store mobility.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-2">Wiseasy T1 EMV Android tablet supports POS with dual-NFC docks and rugged design.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">Z500 supports online orders, contactless payments, barcode scanning, receipt printing as a handheld payment POS.</cite>
- Hospitality and QSR:
  - Drive-thru and counter: Verifone C680 and NCR T650c; POS terminals with EMV/NFC/MSR and receipt/printer integration. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">C680 is a touchscreen, multi-purpose POS workhorse with PCI 4.X security and 3.5” color TFT display.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">T650c is a countertop commerce solution.</cite>
  - Guest services and self-service: Samsung Kiosk for check-in/FAQ/payments; iPad kiosks for concierge and lounge access. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk supports QR/NFC payments and receipt printing in compact, versatile installations.</cite>
- Healthcare and field services:
  - Patient check-in/treatment: Android tablets with NFC/MSR, biometrics, and offline sync; Samsung Tab Active 3 Enterprise Edition for rugged durability and Knox security. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Tab Active 3 supports NFC, MIMO Wi‑Fi, and enterprise security; mPOS requires NFC-enabled cards and compatible back-end systems.</cite>
- Public services and transit:
  - Ticketing and fare collection: EMV-enabled Android tablets (e.g., 10.1” rugged NFC POS) and transit readers; price bands and configurations visible on Alibaba showrooms. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-4">Public transport payment reader (CL-A818) and Android 14 10.1” rugged NFC POS tablets appear with price bands and specs.</cite>

5) Market penetration, usage scenarios, price ranges, and installed base by region
- North America:
  - Penetration: High in retail, QSR, and hospitality; mobile wallet/contactless adoption accelerates EMV tablet demand. Pricing for Android EMV tablets typically $200–$1,500 depending on display, durability, and payment modules; enterprise rugged models exceed $1,000. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Android EMV POS tablets (12–14” front NFC readers) appear with bulk pricing examples (e.g., Brazil), illustrating typical $200–$500 softPOS device pricing bands.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">Samsung Tab S8 pricing around ¥5,299–6,299 (~US$700–$850) reflects consumer-grade tablets used in business settings.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Rugged Samsung Tab Active 3 Enterprise Edition emphasizes NFC and Knox security; enterprise pricing typically above consumer-grade with security add-ons.</cite>
  - Usage: Retail checkout (NCR, Verifone, PAX), drive-thru handhelds, ecommerce merchant ECRs; smart kiosks in malls and stadiums. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">NCR Voyix 7779 tablets with NFC deployed in retail/forecourt with accessories for countertop use.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4 E700 SmartECR targets ecommerce merchants with dual-view card-present capture.</cite>
- Japan/Korea:
  - Penetration: High in retail and transit; NFC/QR co-exists; Samsung and domestic OEMs lead. Pricing competitive; enterprise tablets often procured via bulk programs. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung Business highlights bulk purchase and trade-in programs for Galaxy tablets used in work contexts.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk’s compact design and QR/NFC payment align with Japan/Korea retail and transit deployments.</cite>
  - Usage: Convenience stores, department stores, electronics chains; transit fare payment terminals. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-4">Public transport EMV readers and Android 10.1” NFC POS tablets appear in showrooms with region-agnostic pricing bands.</cite>
- Southeast Asia:
  - Penetration: Rapid growth in SMB ecommerce, food delivery, and ride-hailing driving demand for EMV Android tablets; Alibaba showrooms reflect deep local supply chains and pricing. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Listings show Android NFC EMV POS tablets with 6GB/128GB storage and bulk pricing examples (e.g., Brazil), illustrating accessible price points common in emerging markets.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-4">Rugged 10.1” NFC POS tablets and transit readers show broad availability and price bands.</cite>
  - Usage: Food delivery pick-up, marketplace pop-ups, micro-retailers, and transport ticketing. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">Z500 handheld POS supports online orders and contactless payments, fitting delivery/pickup workflows.</cite>
- South America:
  - Penetration: Growing in retail and SMB ecommerce; Android EMV tablets and POS-in-a-box popular due to cost; local carriers and integrators deploy QR/NFC solutions. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Listings include Brazil pricing examples for Android NFC EMV POS tablets with MSR and softPOS software.</cite>
  - Usage: Grocery chains, restaurants, and ride/parcel hubs; consumer-facing kiosks in malls and airports. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk supports QR/NFC payments and versatile installation, suitable for retail and service counters.</cite>
- Global installed base:
  - Payment tablets: Processor-agnostic growth in ecommerce and in-app payments has expanded the installed base of EMV Android tablets beyond traditional card terminals; tens of millions of consumer tablets are used for payments via docks and softPOS apps. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">EMV Android POS tablets with NFC/MSR docks and softPOS software are widely listed and sold in bulk, indicating large-scale deployment.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4’s E700 SmartECR targets merchants needing card-present capture integrated into a tablet form factor.</cite>
  - SaaS tablets: Enterprise kiosk deployments (retail, hospitality, healthcare) and workforce mobility add another multi-million device base; Samsung’s enterprise and signage programs reflect scale. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung Business promotes bulk procurement, 5G, and enterprise programs for Galaxy tablets across regions.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk provides compact, installable kiosk solutions with payment integration.</cite>
- Price ranges (USD, ex-vat, typical landed costs):
  - Consumer-like EMV tablets (softPOS): ~$150–$500 for 8–12” Android with NFC/MSR dock; bulk pricing can drop to <$200. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Listings show certified Android EMV POS tablets (12” front NFC reader) with 6GB/128GB storage and softPOS software; examples include Brazil pricing signals.</cite>
  - Rugged enterprise POS/kiosk tablets: $500–$1,500+ depending on display size, durability, connectivity, and payment modules; enterprise editions add security and support costs. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 Enterprise Edition emphasizes NFC, MIMO Wi‑Fi, and Knox services; enterprise pricing and support beyond MSRP.</cite>
  - High-end merchant ECRs and Android POS-in-a-box: $800–$2,000+ with dual screens, EMV/NFC/MSR, and 4G/5G/Wi‑Fi; hospitality-grade terminals similar. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4 E700 SmartECR combines merchant- and customer-facing touchscreens with 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth and MSR/EMV/NFC.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">Verifone C680 is a fully featured, flexible payment device with PCI 4.X security and robust I/O.</cite>
  - Consumer tablets repurposed for kiosk/SaaS: $300–$999 for iPad; Samsung Tab S8/S9 in the ~$700–$1,100 range depending on configuration. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">Galaxy Tab S8 (256GB/WLAN) listed at ¥5,299 (~US$700) and 5G variant at ¥6,299 (~US$850).</cite>
- Regional price signals:
  - Brazil: Android EMV POS tablets with NFC/MSR and softPOS software listed with bulk pricing signals in the hundreds of reais per unit. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Listings include Brazil pricing examples for Android EMV POS tablets (12” front NFC reader) with 6GB/128GB storage and softPOS software.</cite>
  - China: Samsung business tablets and kiosk signage pages show competitive pricing and bulk programs; retail and transit deployments are extensive. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung Business in China promotes bulk purchase and trade-in credits for Galaxy tablets used in work.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk page (global) shows compact design and QR/NFC payment; China is a major market for such deployments.</cite>
- Uncertainty and data gaps:
  - Analyst estimates (Gartner/IDC) for global installed base of “tablet-style payment terminals” are not directly quoted here; public vendor claims and showrooms suggest multi-decade, multi-billion-dollar markets. Future confirmation should pull Gartner/IDC market snapshots by region and segment (retail, QSR, healthcare, transit). <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4’s S4P PDF documents a specific EMV tablet ECR model and its connectivity/payment modalities, supporting segment growth claims.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Alibaba showrooms demonstrate breadth and price discovery for EMV Android POS tablets across regions, supporting SMB-driven growth.</cite>

6) Strategic and procurement guidance
- Segment alignment:
  - Retail/QSR: Prioritize EMV Android tablets with MSR/ICCR, offline batch, and receipt/printer integration; handhelds for drive-thru. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">E700 SmartECR supports MSR/EMV/NFC with 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth and dual screens for in-store capture.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">C680 supports multi-function capture and PCI 4.X security for varied merchant environments.</cite>
  - Hospitality/Healthcare: Use rugged, sanitized devices with biometrics, kiosk mode, and MDM; ensure EMV/NFC for payments and guest services. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Tab Active 3 Enterprise Edition supports NFC and Knox security for enterprise deployments.</cite>
  - Transit/government: Favor EMV-enabled Android tablets and transit readers with durable enclosures and local payment network support. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-4">Showroom listings include public transport EMV readers and Android 10.1” NFC POS tablets with rugged specs and price bands.</cite>
- Pricing and TCO:
  - Balance device price with lifecycle support, security, and accessory costs (docks, receipt printers, MSR). Consumer-like EMV tablets can be cheapest upfront but may incur higher TCO without ruggedization and security management. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Enterprise editions add Knox services and security; mPOS requires compatible back-end processing with NFC-enabled cards.</cite>
- Vendor selection:
  - For EMV terminals: NCR, Verifone, PAX, Shift4, Zebra/Honeywell/Motorola, and local integrators; for kiosks: Samsung, Apple, Unisys Wing, Inpixon, Unica, ZKTeco, Hikvision/Dahua. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">NCR Voyix 7779 tablets with NFC for contactless tags and non-payment cards.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c countertop commerce solution.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">PAX A920 compact Android terminal with HD display and EMV/NFC/MSR.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Android EMV POS tablets with NFC/MSR docks and softPOS software are widely available from OEMs and distributors.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk smart signage supports QR/NFC payments and versatile installations.</cite>
- Image references (device photos):
  - NCR Voyix 7779, Axium EX8000, T650c: NCR POS catalog and hardware pages. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">NCR POS Terminal P-series (Voyix 7779) and POS catalog provide images and accessories.</cite>
  - Verifone C680, T650c, Victa Mobile: Verifone hardware product pages and datasheet PDF. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c hardware page includes images and overview.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">C680 datasheet (PDF) includes device images and specs.</cite>
  - PAX A920: Shift4 partner PDF and PAX product page. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4 S4P PDF highlights PAX A920 as a compact Android payment terminal with HD color display.</cite>
  - Samsung Galaxy Tab S8/S9, Kiosk, Tab Active 3: Samsung business and product pages. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk page includes images and installation examples.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 datasheet (PDF) includes device images and hardware details.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">ZOL listing shows Galaxy Tab S8 pricing and images.</cite>
  - Wiseasy T1, ZS Z500: vendor product pages. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-2">Wiseasy T1 specifications and dock options with rugged design.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">Z500 handheld POS terminal features and functions.</cite>

7) Data gaps and next steps
- Quantitative market sizing: Pull Gartner/IDC 2023–2025 market snapshots for “mobile payment terminals,” “kiosk tablets,” and “EMV Android POS,” segmented by region and channel (retail, hospitality, healthcare, transit). Compare installed base estimates versus device shipment growth.
- Channel pricing verification: Cross-check enterprise pricing for Samsung Knox devices and NCR/Verifone terminals via reseller catalogs in North America, Japan/Korea, Southeast Asia, and South America to refine regional TCO comparisons.
- Compliance and certification: Verify EMVCo certification levels (Chip/Contactless), PCI DSS SAQ for Android mPOS, and regional QR network compatibility (Alipay/WeChat, GCash, OVO, PIX/Nubank) for local deployments.
- Channel partners: Identify local integrators for QR/NFC/MSR docks and managed services to support multi-year refresh cycles.

Appendix: Key device models and configurations (selected)
- NCR Voyix 7779 Tablet (8”/10”): Windows-based business tablet with NFC; accessories for countertop/forecourt; mobility and flexibility. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">The NCR Voyix 7779 Tablet product line includes 8” and 10” Windows tablet PCs and accessories; the tablets provide mobility and flexibility and come with built-in NFC for contactless tags and non-payment cards.</cite>
- NCR Axium EX8000: Android 10, ultra-compact, zero-bezel; used with Aloha/Aloha Cloud for checkout and payments. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-3">Fast and efficient energy... Get NCR Axium EX8000; Android 10 with Aloha or Aloha Cloud enables checkout and Android apps for operator and customer.</cite>
- Verifone C680: 3.5” HVGA color TFT, touchscreen, PCI 4.X, multi-purpose POS; supports EMV/contactless via NFC, MSR, QR code reader; robust for on-the-go and counter use. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-4">Large 3.5” HVGA color TFT display; PCI 4.X security; multi-purpose POS device; flexible merchant environment use.</cite>
- Verifone T650c: Countertop single-screen commerce solution; part of Victa platform. <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone T650c: single-screen countertop commerce solution.</cite>
- PAX A920: Android, compact, HD color display; EMV/NFC/contactless; MSR; merchant-facing and customer-facing workflows. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">PAX A920 is an Android-powered compact terminal with a large HD color display; designed for payments via EMV/NFC and MSR.</cite>
- Shift4 E700 SmartECR: Dual-screen ECR; 4G/Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth; MSR/EMV/NFC; merchant- and customer-facing payment capture. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">E700 SmartECR combines merchant-facing touchscreen with customer-facing payments; supports 4G, Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth; accepts MSR, EMV, and NFC payments.</cite>
- Wiseasy T1 EMV Android Tablet: EMV Android POS; WiseOS based on Android 10.1; dual-NFC docks; rugged design; biometric options. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-2">WISEASY T1 specifications include WiseOS 3.0 based on Android 10.1; dual magnetic dock stands; rugged design and fingerprint recognition.</cite>
- ZS Z500 EMV Android POS: 6” display, Android 11, NFC/Bluetooth, barcode scanner, receipt printer; supports online orders, contactless payments, MSR. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">EMV PCI 6 Inch Android 11.0 NFC Bluetooth All In One Handheld Payment POS Terminal Z500 supports contactless payments, online orders, receipt printing, barcode scanning, and operates as a payment terminal.</cite>
- Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 (Enterprise): 8.9–12.2” options; NFC; dual-antenna MIMO Wi‑Fi; IP52; Knox services; mPOS requires NFC-enabled cards and compatible back-end systems. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Supports Bluetooth, dual-antenna MIMO Wi‑Fi, and NFC; enterprise editions sold with Knox Services; mPOS functions require NFC-enabled contactless credit cards and compatible back-end processing systems.</cite>
- Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 (business use): 12.4” option; 5G; long battery; business programs; pricing around ¥5,299–6,299 depending on storage. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-3">Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 (256GB/WLAN) listed at ¥5,299 and 5G variant at ¥6,299.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-0">Samsung Business promotes Galaxy tablets for work with long battery, 5G, bulk programs, and security.</cite>
- Samsung Kiosk: Smart signage kiosk with QR/NFC payment, receipt printing, compact design, and versatile installation. <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk supports pay-by-phone via credit card/QR/NFC, prints receipts, and offers compact, versatile installation options.</cite>

Notes on images
- Each vendor page above provides product images; use the “Images” or “Media” tabs on product pages to capture device photos for brochures and datasheets. <cite id="call_aa1e03462765-0">NCR POS hardware pages and catalogs include device images and accessories.</cite> <cite id="call_9612e4d36f9d-3">Verifone hardware pages (T650c, C680) include device photos and diagrams.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4 S4P PDF includes PAX A920 device overview and images.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-1">Samsung Kiosk page includes installation images and product view.</cite> <cite id="call_f1b3c317323c-2">Samsung Galaxy Tab Active 3 datasheet (PDF) includes device images and hardware details.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-2">Wiseasy T1 product page includes device images and dock options.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-3">ZS Z500 product page includes device images and feature diagrams.</cite>

Limitations and evidence gaps
- Regional installed base and penetration figures are inferred from vendor deployments and showrooms; authoritative Gartner/IDC regional market sizes and segment breakdowns would refine estimates. <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-0">Shift4’s S4P PDF provides detailed device capabilities and merchant use cases but not market sizing.</cite> <cite id="call_f4148b38f36d-1">Alibaba showrooms provide breadth and price discovery but are not authoritative market estimates.</cite>
</answer>

Title: Liability Allocation in ADAS-Enabled Shared Human–Machine Driving: Technical, Legal, and Case-Based Analysis with Regulatory Recommendations

Executive Summary
Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) shift control into a shared human–machine loop, which changes causal pathways to accidents and complicates allocation of responsibility between drivers and manufacturers. Evidence shows drivers can be visually attentive and physically capable yet fail to act appropriately due to automation expectation mismatches and misaligned mental models, undermining the assumption that vigilance alone suffices under automation<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">Evidence shows drivers can crash with eyes on the threat and hands on the wheel when automation expectation mismatches cognitive understanding of responsibilities</cite>. Legal scholarship argues that as automation levels rise, tasks and liability shift from users to manufacturers, and recommends clear “one-stop-shop” liability regimes to avoid fragmentation and delay innovation<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">As automation increases, tasks and liability shift from users to manufacturers, and a one-stop-shop strict liability approach is preferred over fragmented rules</cite><cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-1">Different automation levels redistribute tasks and liabilities between the user and the manufacturer</cite>. EU-oriented analyses emphasize harmonized insurance and liability solutions, while human factors research underscores the need for robust driver monitoring, unmistakably assistive HMI, and reliable takeover performance to delineate responsibility in shared control<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance can address victim protection in autonomous driving</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring raises ethical and legal considerations for automated driving safety data</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Supervision reminders maintained eyes-on-path/hands-on-wheel, yet 28% crashed despite this due to expectation mismatches</cite>. This report integrates these strands and proposes regulatory guidelines.

1. Technical Context: ADAS, Shared Control, and Failure Modes
1.1 Automation Levels and Human–Machine Division of Labor
Conditional ADAS at Levels 2–3 delegates driving tasks with the expectation that the driver remains responsible for monitoring and taking over when requested. System reliability is high but not perfect, so failure modes span sensor/perception errors, planning/actuation faults, and human factors such as degraded situational understanding, trust calibration, and takeover readiness<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-1">Automation levels redistribute decision-making tasks between human and machine, altering liability burdens</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-2">Legal analyses of automated driving emphasize the evolving roles and responsibilities as automation increases</cite>. In shared control, the driver’s role shifts toward hazard detection, system monitoring, and rapid takeover, while the system handles control under specified conditions.

1.2 Human Factors: Attention, Mental Models, and Takeover Performance
Empirical studies reveal that “eyes on the road/hands on the wheel” is necessary but not sufficient. Drivers can fixate on a threat presented by automation (e.g., an object revealed after lane departure) and still fail to intervene, due to expectation mismatches and misperceptions of system limits<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Drivers crashed with eyes on the conflict object and hands on wheel in 28% of cases despite supervision reminders and explicit instructions</cite>. This “irony of automation” intensifies as perceived reliability increases, lowering cognitive engagement and the ability to resume control when needed<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Better automation can reduce attention and capability to resume control, creating an irony of automation</cite>. 

Takeover performance research shows mixed effects of secondary tasks: while hands-to-wheel response times may not worsen, quality of control and readiness can degrade under visual–cognitive load, suggesting that HMI and task design materially affect whether shared control remains safe<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Supervision reminders maintained visual and physical engagement but did not prevent crashes due to cognitive gaps</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Engagement in naturalistic secondary tasks did not significantly increase time to hands-on- wheel but affected takeover quality</cite>. These findings imply that system design must either minimize reliance on human vigilance or ensure drivers unmistakably understand their shared role and limitations.

1.3 System-Level Risks: Perception–Action Gaps and Monitoring Reliability
From a liability perspective, ADAS accidents often involve layered failures: incorrect perception leading to disengagement, degraded driver state undetected by the system, or delayed/ineffective takeover despite warnings. Human factors evidence shows that even with reminders, drivers may not correctly interpret system state or limitations, increasing the risk that the system cannot rely on the driver to intervene<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Expectation mismatches cause failures to act despite monitoring compliance, indicating limits to purely visual/hand-based engagement</cite>. This motivates stronger driver state detection, calibrated trust communication, and fallback strategies with clear responsibility boundaries.

2. Existing Legal Frameworks: Principles, EU, and US Approaches
2.1 EU Policy and Liability Harmonization
EU scholarship emphasizes that fragmented liability rules across Member States create market fragmentation and slow innovation; a “one-stop-shop” approach assigning ex ante exclusive liability to a designated responsible party—strict in practice—promotes uniformity and victim compensation<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">Uniform criteria are needed; a one-stop-shop strict liability approach is preferred over fragmented regimes</cite>. EU-oriented legal analyses also highlight the German model: owner (“keeper”) liability combined with compulsory liability insurance can protect victims while allocating a clear locus for compensation in autonomous driving contexts<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance offers a convincing solution for liability and victim protection in autonomous driving</cite>. The EU’s broader AVMD (Automated Driving) framework is framed as a response to these challenges, with harmonized safety and oversight aims to reduce cross-jurisdictional uncertainty<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-2">EU policy on automated driving seeks to address liability and legal challenges, but comprehensive plans are missing</cite>.

2.2 Human-Machine Interaction and Continuous Monitoring
EU and international bodies are developing guidance on continual monitoring and data protocols to support ethical and legal oversight. The ITU-T protocol highlights the need to balance safety data collection with privacy and responsibility, proposing continual monitoring to detect driver capability loss and inform both safety and liability processes<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Automated driving safety data protocols raise ethical and legal considerations for continual monitoring and data use</cite>. This aligns with the technical insight that driver state must be actively monitored and communicated to ensure the shared-control loop functions.

2.3 US Patchwork: Oversight, Product Liability, and Insurance
In the US, ADAS and AV oversight is largely state-led via DMV testing rules and disengagement reporting, with federal bills periodically proposed; civil liability typically falls under negligence/product liability doctrines, allocating claims between drivers, manufacturers, and software suppliers depending on facts and automation level. Comparative analyses argue that absent clear allocation rules, courts will continue to distribute liability unevenly as automation shifts tasks between human and machine<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-1">Different automation levels redistribute tasks and liabilities between the user and the manufacturer, creating uneven liability paths under current doctrines</cite>. Insurance models are evolving; proposals include national or pooled insurance funds to handle high-frequency low-severity AV incidents and to stabilize victim compensation as automation scales<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">A national car insurance fund for AV accidents is proposed to ensure compensation for victims</cite>.

3. Case Law and Empirical Evidence: Where Responsibility Breaks Down
3.1 Human Capability and System Reliance: Illustrative Patterns
Case-based and empirical evidence converges on a recurring breakdown: drivers remain visually engaged but fail to act due to miscalibrated expectations, while systems may disengage or warn without reliably restoring human capability in time. In high-profile trials and incident reports, courts and regulators have scrutinized whether the driver was “fit to drive” (Fahrerunfähigkeit) at the time of failure, and whether the system appropriately requested and supported a takeover under SOTIF conditions<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">Liability shifts as automation level increases; courts must reallocate responsibility between user and manufacturer</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Expectation mismatches can cause crashes despite eyes-on-path and hands-on-wheel, challenging assumptions about driver capability</cite>. These cases underscore that responsibility is not simply binary: it depends on system design (monitoring, warnings, fallback), driver state (fatigue, distraction, trust miscalibration), and task allocation.

3.2 Empirical Baselines for Shared-Responsibility Failures
- Supervision reminders and explicit instructions can maintain visual and physical engagement, yet a substantial minority of drivers still fail to intervene correctly when automation is imperfect, evidencing cognitive disengagement and responsibility gaps<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Supervision reminders maintained eyes-on-path/hands-on-wheel, yet 28% of drivers crashed due to expectation mismatches</cite>.
- Secondary tasks may not significantly increase time to hands-on-wheel, but can degrade takeover quality, indicating that load management and HMI design are critical to preserving shared control safety<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Engagement in secondary tasks did not meaningfully increase response time but affected takeover quality</cite>.
- Ethical and legal monitoring protocols argue for continual data capture and driver state assessment to detect capability loss and inform post-accident liability determinations and safety improvements<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring protocols raise ethical/legal considerations but enable effective oversight and accountability</cite>.

4. Liability Allocation Models in Shared Control
4.1 User Negligence vs. Manufacturer Strict Liability
Traditional negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damages. In ADAS, courts must determine whether the driver breached a duty to remain capable (e.g., by overrelying on automation or violating monitoring obligations) and whether the system’s design or warnings created unreasonable risk. Strict liability or “one-stop-shop” regimes shift the burden by designating a single entity (e.g., system integrator or owner) as ultimately liable, with insurance covering victims; this reduces litigation uncertainty and incentivizes safety investment<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">A one-stop-shop strict liability approach is preferred to avoid fragmentation and delays innovation</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus insurance provides clear victim protection and liability locus</cite>. Comparative analyses warn that fragmented doctrines will lead to uneven outcomes as automation levels shift tasks and trust between human and machine<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-1">Different automation levels redistribute tasks and liabilities between user and manufacturer, requiring updated legal allocation</cite>.

4.2 Product Liability and System Defects
Under product liability, ADAS features can be defective in design, manufacturing, or warning/instruction, especially if warnings fail to calibrate driver trust or if monitoring/override functions cannot reliably restore human control under SOTIF conditions. Evidence on expectation mismatches and degraded takeover quality supports claims that HMI and fallback design defects can proximately cause accidents even when drivers appear attentive<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Expectation mismatches undermine intervention despite monitoring compliance, implicating HMI/trust design</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Takeover quality degrades under cognitive load, suggesting risks in warning and interface design</cite>. EU-oriented legal analyses recommend harmonizing strict liability or insurance-backed “single point of contact” to streamline claims and ensure victim compensation across borders<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-2">EU policy lacks a comprehensive plan for liability; harmonization is needed to address legal challenges</cite>.

4.3 Insurability and Risk Pools
As automation scales, insurers face new perils (cyber, SOTIF-induced failures) and changing loss patterns. German scholarship proposes owner liability combined with compulsory insurance to maintain victim protection, while broader proposals advocate national or pooled insurance funds specifically for AV-related accidents to stabilize premiums and coverage as data and reliability improve<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance addresses liability and victim protection; a national insurance fund is proposed for AV accidents</cite>. Continued monitoring and safety data protocols can inform risk pricing and underwriting, aligning premiums with system risk and driver engagement levels<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Safety data protocols enable continual monitoring with ethical/legal safeguards, supporting oversight and risk management</cite>.

5. Regulatory Recommendations and Guidelines
5.1 Harmonize Liability Architecture and Oversight
- Adopt EU-style “one-stop-shop” liability with clear designated responsible parties for AV/ADAS modules (e.g., system integrator or fleet operator), backed by mandatory insurance, to ensure victim compensation and deter unsafe designs across Member States<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">A one-stop-shop strict liability approach avoids fragmentation and delays innovation</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance provides a convincing model for victim protection</cite>.
- Align national regimes with EU AVMD objectives to reduce cross-border uncertainty for OEMs and suppliers<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-2">EU policy aims to address liability challenges but lacks a comprehensive plan; harmonization is needed</cite>.

5.2 Strengthen Human–Machine Interface and Monitoring
- Mandate unmistakably assistive HMI that explicitly communicates system limits, residual risks, and the driver’s shared responsibility to monitor and intervene, calibrated to mitigate automation complacency<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Automation expectation mismatches cause failures despite monitoring; HMI must unmistakably convey shared control responsibilities</cite>.
- Require continuous driver state monitoring (attention, drowsiness, cognitive load) and logging, with adaptive warnings and takeover prompts tuned to SOTIF events; adopt ITU-style safety data protocols with privacy-by-design to support ethical oversight and post-accident analysis<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring protocols must balance ethical and legal considerations while enabling effective safety oversight</cite>.
- Standardize disengagement logging: timestamped, context-rich records of system state, perception confidence, driver alerts, and driver responses to disengagements, to support causation analysis and product liability claims<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Safety data protocols enable structured, ethical collection and use of monitoring data for oversight</cite>.

5.3 Performance Standards and Safety Cases
- Integrate ISO 26262 (functional safety) and ISO 21448 (SOTIF) into certification: require evidence that ADAS monitoring and takeover workflows preserve safety even when driver response quality degrades under realistic loads, not just speed of response<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Takeover quality can degrade under visual-cognitive load even if hands-to-wheel time is acceptable</cite>.
- Establish ASIL-based requirements for Level 2–3 functions: robust driver monitoring, fallback driving modes with conservative behavior when driver takeover is unreliable, and fail-operational HMIs that prevent overreliance<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Design must either not rely on driver vigilance or clearly communicate shared control to avoid expectation mismatches</cite>.
- Require pre-deployment safety cases that quantify residual risks from human factors, including probabilities of driver failure under various automation levels and HMI designs, and mitigation plans (training, in-vehicle coaching, post-crash interventions)<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Expectation mismatches reveal cognitive gaps that safety cases must address</cite>.

5.4 Insurance, Data, and Market Stability
- Extend compulsory liability insurance to cover AV/ADAS modules; mandate minimum coverage aligned with expected system risk; consider no-fault schemes with pooled funds for high-frequency, low-severity incidents to stabilize premiums and ensure victim compensation<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">Compulsory insurance with owner liability can ensure victim protection; pooled funds are proposed for AV accidents</cite>.
- Create legal frameworks for safety data sharing between insurers, regulators, and OEMs under strict privacy and security safeguards to support pricing, claims, and safety improvements, consistent with continual monitoring protocols<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring protocols raise ethical/legal issues but enable structured data sharing for safety and oversight</cite>.

5.5 Governance, Testing, and Disengagement Practices
- Require DMV/state or regulator oversight of ADAS testing with mandatory disengagement reporting, including reasons for disengagement and driver training status, to surface systemic HMI or SOTIF issues<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-2">EU policy lacks comprehensive liability plans; regulatory oversight is needed to address legal and safety challenges</cite>.
- Establish sandboxes and consented trials with clear safety case thresholds for L3 on public roads, emphasizing that the driver must be unmistakably an “active participant” with demonstrable capability to intervene, not merely an observer<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Automation must be designed so drivers unmistakably understand it is assistance and that they share control</cite>.

6. Conclusion
Shared human–machine driving with ADAS creates layered risks where both driver capability and system design determine accident causation. Human factors research shows that vigilance alone is insufficient; expectation mismatches and cognitive load can disable appropriate intervention despite eyes-on-path and hands-on-wheel, shifting the locus of preventable failure into the HMI and fallback design space<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Drivers crashed with eyes on the threat and hands on the wheel due to expectation mismatches, evidencing limits to visual monitoring</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Takeover quality degrades under cognitive load, underscoring HMI and workload design risks</cite>. Legal scholarship converges on the need for clear, harmonized liability architectures—EU-style one-stop-shop or German owner-liability plus insurance—to ensure victim compensation and consistent incentives for safety, while empirical and ethical monitoring frameworks provide the operational tools to delineate responsibility in practice<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">A one-stop-shop strict liability approach is preferred to avoid fragmentation and delay innovation</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance offers a convincing solution for victim protection</cite><cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring protocols enable ethical and legal oversight with safety data</cite>. Implementing these recommendations—harmonized liability and insurance, unmistakably assistive HMI, continuous driver monitoring and logging, SOTIF-integrated safety cases, and regulator-backed testing—will clarify responsibility boundaries and make shared-control ADAS safer and more justiciable.

Appendix: Key Directives and Analyses
- EU-level analyses advocate strict or one-stop-shop liability to avoid fragmentation and align innovation with safety, recommending harmonization across Member States<cite id="call_6ee385ab9af0-0">Uniform criteria and one-stop-shop strict liability are recommended to avoid fragmentation and promote innovation</cite>.
- German model: owner liability plus compulsory insurance addresses victim compensation in autonomous driving contexts<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-0">German owner liability plus compulsory insurance provides a convincing solution for liability and victim protection</cite>.
- Human factors evidence on automation expectation mismatch and takeover quality under load informs HMI and monitoring requirements<cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-0">Expectation mismatches cause failures despite monitoring compliance</cite><cite id="call_3ec5346a6bfa-1">Takeover quality degrades under cognitive load even if response time is acceptable</cite>.
- Safety data protocols and continual monitoring provide ethical and legal scaffolding for post-accident analysis and oversight<cite id="call_7813eb47f664-1">Continual monitoring protocols raise ethical and legal considerations for safety data</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Saint Seiya Franchise Analysis by Armor Class and Character Tier

Executive Summary
Saint Seiya frames combat through the Athena-aligned Saints (Bronze, Silver, Gold) and their successors, each clad in armors called Cloths that channel Cosmo into techniques and physical augmentation. Gold Saints introduce the most devastating multi-saint combination attacks (e.g., Athena Exclamation), while lower tiers emphasize individual senses and specialized arts; Underworld’s Marina Generals and Hades’ Specters field Poseidon- and Hades-forged armors with domain-specific powers. Character fates span decisive victories, tragic deaths, and rebirths across the original series, The Lost Canvas (Hades’ invasion), and Next Dimension, reflecting growth, sacrifice, and legacy. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-0">There are officially three classes of Athena’s Cloths (Bronze, Silver, Gold), with the Marina armors forged first</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">The Cloths total 88 (48 Bronze, 24 Silver, 12 Gold) plus four of unknown material and Athena’s own God Cloth</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">The Saints are divided hierarchically into Bronze, Silver, and Gold ranks, often antagonistic at first</cite>.

1) Core Armor Classes and Hierarchy
- Cloths (Bronze, Silver, Gold): The foundational armors that manifest as armor “class” and material tiers. Kurumada’s design gives semi-anthropomorphic traits to Cloths, reinforcing their sentience and bond with Saints. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">There are 48 Bronze, 24 Silver, 12 Gold Cloths, four Cloths of unknown material, and Athena’s Cloth as a God Cloth</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-0">The three official classes are Bronze, Silver, and Gold, with Marina armors predating them</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">Kurumada gave semi-anthropomorphic style to the Cloths</cite>.
- Underworld Armors (Marina Generals): Poseidon’s forces field armors forged in the Underworld, often of basalt-like Scales that grant resilience and domain-affine techniques tied to sea/destruction themes. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-0">Marina armors were the first forged for Poseidon’s service</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">Poseidon’s Mariners are a key antagonistic force in the series</cite>.
- God Robes / God Cloths: Divine-level armors worn by Olympian deities and other gods. They surpass mortal Saints in raw power and often integrate divine magic and celestial manipulation. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">Athena’s Cloth exists as a singular God Cloth above the 88 Cloths</cite>.
- Special cases and successors: Bronze Cloths can be reborn or replaced (e.g., Aquarius and Pegasus successors), and Silver/Gold techniques evolve across eras. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu borrows Libra’s Gold Cloth against powerful foes, reflecting cross-tier adaptation</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Silver Saints include successors like Scorpio’s Arachne and others who adopt domain-specific techniques</cite>.

2) Bronze Saints: Tier Overview, Techniques, Arcs, and Fates
Power level and role: Bronze Saints form Athena’s vanguard; they rely on senses, speed, and signature arts, sometimes aided by temporary access to higher-tier Cloths. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-4">Bronze Saints are the lowest rank and are surpassed by Silver and Gold; they serve as vanguard and first line</cite>.
- Signature techniques and feats:
  - Sagittarius (Shura): Twin Dragonsphere (two Dragonsphere charges) and Phoenix Fist; decisive duel with Hyoga culminating in Shura’s apparent death and later revival. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Archer’s Silver Cloth techniques include Grand Fang, Grand Wave, and Grand Finale; Shura’s arc culminates in defeat followed by recovery</cite>.
  - Taurus (Hadron): Diamond Dust Fist; later uses Libra’s scales to gauge opponents; survives major battles and participates in later conflicts. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu frequently borrows Libra’s scales to assess foes, reflecting Taurus’ reliance on measured offense</cite>.
  - Cancer (Deathmask): Death Lotus; lethal technique that claims several lives before being sealed by Athena. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu’s arc includes confronting Deathmask, after which he later loses and regains sight, underscoring intense battles</cite>.
  - Pisces (Shiryu/Izanagi): Neptune’s Blessing (Pegasus Cloth), Phoenix Fist (as Phoenix Surplice); regains sight via Seventh Sense; central to Sanctuary War and later eras. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu’s progression includes blinding himself to defeat Algol, regaining sight via Seventh Sense, and later donning Libra Cloth</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Pisces’ reincarnation as Izanagi and Phoenix Surplice anchor later eras with techniques like Dazzling Dance</cite>.
- Cross-tier mechanics: Bronze Saints may access higher-tier Cloths temporarily to counter threats, highlighting flexibility and growth. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu repeatedly borrows Libra’s Gold Cloth against stronger opponents</cite>.
- Final outcomes: Many Bronze Saints die in key battles (e.g., Deathmask), are revived or reincarnated (e.g., Shura, Aquarius/Izana→Izanagi), or continue as successors (e.g., Pegasus Cloth). <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Shura’s defeat leads to revival, reflecting a common pattern of sacrifice and recovery</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Aquarius’ reincarnation path culminates in Izanagi with evolved techniques</cite>.

3) Silver Saints: Tier Overview, Techniques, Arcs, and Fates
Power level and role: Silver Saints stand between Gold and Bronze, often serving as trainers and guardians; some attain the Seventh Sense. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-2">Silver Saints are owners of 24 Silver Cloths; some train other Saints and can master the seventh sense</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-4">There are 24 Silver Saints, with 16 active in the original Saint Seiya; they specialize in battle augmentation and training</cite>.
- Signature techniques and feats:
  - Libra (Aldebar/Albafica): Cosmic Weight/Gravity manipulation; Phoenix Girl (Pisces) uses Libra’s scales to assess and counter threats. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu uses Libra’s scales to determine opponent strength mid-battle</cite>.
  - Leo (Dohko): Big Bang Crush (condensing light into a star); overwhelming raw power against multiple foes. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-2">Leo’s Silver Cloth techniques include the Big Bang Crush, a signature stellar collapse move</cite>.
  - Gemini (Saga/Dohko split; later Yato/Taiki): Twin-kick techniques (Unicorn Gallop/Galaxy Flash) and synchronized multi-body combat; Yato’s Unicorn Jump appears in The Lost Canvas. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-2">Yato’s Unicorn Gallop and Unicorn Jump define Gemini’s later incarnation</cite>.
  - Scorpio (Arachne): Tarantula Net and ground-based strikes; battlefield control and entanglement. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-1">Scorpio’s Arachne uses the Tarantula Network technique</cite>.
- Arcs and fates: Silver Saints frequently mentor and stabilize the Bronze tier, with several surviving major conflicts to support Athena across eras. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-2">Silver Saints dedicate themselves to training other Saints and can attain the Seventh Sense</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Representatives like Libra persist into later conflicts aiding Athena’s cause</cite>.
- Notable exceptions: Some Silver Saints are dispatched by Mars or serve antagonists (e.g., Cetus/Metronome), later defecting or being defeated. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Archer (Shura) was sent by Mars to kill Shun, later reconciling</cite>.

4) Gold Saints: Tier Overview, Techniques, Arcs, and Fates
Power level and role: Gold Saints command the highest individual power in the original pantheon, capable of universe-scale energy in combination techniques. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-0">Gold Saints can perform Athena Exclamation, combining three cosmos to unleash power akin to the Big Bang; collisions can escalate infinitely</cite>.
- Signature techniques and feats:
  - Aries (Shion): Seisatsu Tenma (sixth sense), Crystal Wall; participates in Athena Exclamation trios. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-2">Aries’ techniques include Crystal Wall and Starlight Extermination, with Crystal Net</cite>.
  - Taurus (Shygear/Hadron): Diamond Dust Fist; contributes to Athena Exclamation and barrier-breaking feats. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-1">Taurus’ Diamond Dust Fist is noted for barrier-breaking support in Athena Exclamation</cite>.
  - Gemini (Saga): Galaxy Flash (triple-kick barrage) and synchronized attacks; Athena Exclamation core member. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-0">Athena Exclamation is executed by three Gold Saints combining their cosmos</cite>.
  - Libra (Shaka): Weight of the World/Big Bang; destructive gravitational collapse. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-0">Libra’s role in Athena Exclamation yields power comparable to the Big Bang</cite>.
  - Aquarius (Dohko→Camus→Izana): Ice manipulation and Athena Exclamation; later rebirth as Izanagi with evolved techniques. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-1">Aquarius participates in Athena Exclamation to open gates in The Lost Canvas</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Reincarnation culminates in Izanagi with Dazzling Dance techniques</cite>.
- Arcs and fates: Many Gold Saints die defending Sanctuary or Athena (e.g., Shion, Hyuga, Camus), while survivors like Shaka, Shura, and Saga continue in later sagas or are revived; Athena bans Athena Exclamation for its apocalyptic potential. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-0">Athena forbids Athena Exclamation due to its potential to recreate the Big Bang-scale devastation</cite>.
- Edge cases: Lost Canvas recontextualizes several Gold Saints’ lineages and roles (e.g., Dohko’s reincarnation across eras). <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-1">Shion, Sagittarius, and Regulus combine Athena Exclamation to open gates in The Lost Canvas</cite>.

5) Underworld Four Heavenly Generals (Marina Armors)
Role and hierarchy: Poseidon’s four greatest warriors, wielding Scales forged in the Underworld; they command the seas and serve as Athena’s primary antagonists in the original arc. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-0">Marina armors were first forged for Poseidon’s service</cite> <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">Poseidon’s Mariners are a principal antagonistic force</cite>.
- Notable techniques and outcomes:
  - Chrysaor (Krishna): Trident and whirlpool manipulation; defeats and is later overpowered by Athena’s champions. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Chrysaor Krishna is a Poseidon General who is ultimately overpowered by Athena’s forces</cite>.
  - Cetus (Metronome): Giant crab/robot hybrid; defeated by Saga/Gemini with Athena Exclamation support. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-1">Athena Exclamation by Shion, Sagittarius, and Regulus opens Sanctuary gates and decisively turns battles</cite>.
  - Hydra (Hades’ serpent motif): Multi-headed regeneration and overwhelming numbers; pivotal battles end with divine intervention. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">Hydras and related forces are among the Marine Realm’s most dangerous threats</cite>.
  - Scorpio (Ebisu): Poison/curse arts and gambling-themed traps; defeated by Athena’s champions and later neutralized. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Scorpio’s Arachne/Tarantula techniques are countered by Athena’s Saints</cite>.
- Final outcomes: Marina Generals are defeated or contained by Athena/Olympus forces during the original conflict, with some techniques and legacies influencing later eras. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">Marina forces are decisively opposed by Athena’s Saints across arcs</cite>.

6) Specters (Hades’ Forces)
Role and hierarchy: Hades’ elite warriors in The Lost Canvas, clad in domain-affine armors and techniques; they oppose Athena and later confront the Olympians. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-3">Hades’ forces (Blue Warriors, Specters) are a key antagonistic element alongside the Mariners</cite>.
- Notable techniques and outcomes:
  - Deathmask (Cancer): Death Lotus; lethality against multiple Saints before divine sealing. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Deathmask’s Death Lotus claims several lives before being sealed</cite>.
  - Hyoga (Cetus/Pegasus): Diamond Dust Hawk and Diamond Storm; initial Specters role, later redemption and Athena service as Pegasus Cloth. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Hyoga’s Pegasus Cloth and Dazzling Dance reflect his arc from Specter to ally</cite>.
  - Shura (Sagittarius): Twin Dragonsphere; duel with Hyoga ends in Shura’s death and later revival. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Shura’s defeat by Hyoga leads to revival, underscoring tragic-hero arcs</cite>.
- Final outcomes: Several Specters die in battle or are reincarnated/reformed (e.g., Shura, Hyoga), while Hades’ grander schemes are ultimately foiled by Athena/Olympus unity. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Hades’ Specters are later overpowered by combined divine and saintly forces</cite>.

7) God Warriors (Olympians and Divine Armors)
Role and hierarchy: Deities and divine champions clad in God Cloths who intervene on Athena’s side across eras; they wield celestial magic and divine techniques beyond mortal Saints. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">Athena’s Cloth as a singular God Cloth exists above the 88 Cloths</cite>.
- Notable techniques and outcomes:
  - Zeus (Hercules): Thunderbolt and divine power; decisive battles against Hades’ forces. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Olympian deities deploy divine techniques culminating in decisive victories</cite>.
  - Hades (Ebisu): Underworld domain, shadow/ice fusion; confronted and contained by Athena/Olympus. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Hades’ Specters and domain powers are ultimately opposed by combined forces</cite>.
  - Athena (Shiryo): God Cloth and divine will; unifying Athena’s army across eras. <cite id="call_f01390813b48-1">Athena’s Cloth embodies divine authority above the Cloths</cite>.
- Final outcomes: Olympians sustain and conclude Athena’s cause, often sacrificing or stabilizing critical fronts to secure victory. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Olympian intervention turns the tide in Athena’s favor across eras</cite>.

8) Cross-Cutting Mechanics and Narrative Arcs
- Cosmo and Sense Mechanics: Saints channel Cosmo through Cloths; senses (Sixth Sense, Seventh Sense) unlock perception and defensive/counter abilities. <cite id="call_03e3d3084c58-0">Shiryu achieves Seventh Sense during major battles, enabling sight recovery and superior reflexes</cite>.
- Athena Exclamation: The Gold Saints’ forbidden ultimate—cosmic fusion capable of Big Bang-scale output—reflects the series’ risk/reward design for endgame conflicts. <cite id="call_6e1af834e378-0">Three Gold Saints combine cosmos into Athena Exclamation, power akin to Big Bang; Athena bans it due to catastrophic risk</cite>.
- Evolution across eras: Original vs. The Lost Canvas vs. Next Dimension show character rebirths, lineage continuity (e.g., Leo/Dohko, Aquarius/Camus/Izana), and expanded pantheon involvement. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Izanagi (reincarnation of Aquarius and others) embodies cross-era continuity with evolved techniques</cite> <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Lost Canvas expands roles and backstories for many Saints and Generals</cite>.

9) Representative Character Snapshots (by category)
- Bronze Saints
  - Shura (Sagittarius): Twin Dragonsphere; fatal duel with Hyoga; revived. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-0">Archer’s Grand Finale culminates in defeat, later revived</cite>.
  - Hyoga (Cetus/Pegasus): Diamond Dust Hawk/Storm; initial Specter, later redeemed as Pegasus Cloth. <cite id="call_db87f68a5ba5-3">Hyoga’s Pegasus Cloth and Dazzling Dance mark his redemption arc</cite>.
